articles.title: The Nature of Phonological Impairments in Dyslexia and Stuttering: Evidence from Phonemic, Semantic, and Design Fluency Tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; James H Smith-Spark; Richard Kirkden
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Using executive fluency tasks, the current study investigated whether these challenges reflect phonological representations themselves or access to intact representations during self-reported adults who stutter (AWS) and self-reported dyslexic adults.
Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 self-reported AWS, 62 self-reported dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency, as well as a mouse-drawn version of design fluency. We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity). 
Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected. Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group. Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these findings suggest that, in dyslexia, access to phonological representations is affected. Conversely, stuttering affects the representations themselves. For individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.

articles.title: Developing and Validating a Measurement Scale to Assess Knowledge of Memory and Learning Processes Among Italian Teachers
articles.authors: Francesco Carabba; Ottavia M. Epifania; Demis Basso
articles.abstract:
Knowledge of memory and learning processes may inform teachers’ educational decisions. However, to our knowledge, no psychometrically validated instrument specifically assesses teachers’ procedural knowledge of these processes through realistic classroom scenarios.
This Stage 1 Registered Report aims to develop and validate a scenario-based measure of Italian teachers’ procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.
Approximately 600 Italian teachers, from preschool to upper-secondary education, will be recruited through proportional stratified quota sampling based on sex, geographical area, and school level.
Following two pilot studies and iterative revisions, 30 original items were retained and paired with conceptually matched items to create two intended parallel forms. All participants will complete the 60 multiple-choice items online. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted separately for each form in independent subsamples. Measurement invariance across forms will be examined if corresponding factor structures are supported. Internal consistency will be estimated using Cronbach’s alpha. Mixed-effects logistic regression will examine associations between item-level accuracy and teaching experience, educational attainment, and, among teachers with tertiary qualifications, academic field.
We expect interpretable, replicable factor structures and adequate internal consistency, with measurement invariance providing additional evidence of comparability across forms. Higher accuracy is tentatively expected with higher educational attainment, psycho-pedagogical qualifications, and fewer years of teaching experience.
The study will provide initial evidence on the psychometric properties of the proposed measure. If the findings support its validity and reliability, the instrument could subsequently be used to identify teachers’ knowledge gaps and inform teacher education initiatives.

articles.title: Multimodal processing of chemical representations: advantages of chemistry expertise and inadvertent challenges for learning
articles.authors: Amanda Bongers; Steven Ganescu
articles.abstract: Chemists use verbal and visual representations of molecules to communicate and solve problems, yet little is known about how chemists efficiently interpret them simultaneously with ease. Participants (N = 200) of varied chemistry expertise completed an experiment in which they solved short representation-matching tasks with bond-line structures and IUPAC names of organic molecules. Drawing upon information-processing theory and prior chemistry education research on representational processing efficiency, we examined how expertise and varied task characteristics affected visual scanning efficiency. We recorded participants’ eye movements during the tasks to quantify the extent to which their gaze was focused or exploratory using a metric called stationary gaze entropy. Chemistry experts exhibited more focused gaze within the bond-line structures presented, which suggests that they more efficiently apply more chunk stimuli and activate prior knowledge connecting the representations. By looking at the effects of varied structural features and complexity, we outline inadvertent challenges that chemistry novices may face while processing these representations during chemistry instruction. We offer chemistry instructors suggestions for mitigating demands on their students’ working memory. We also propose avenues for follow-up research that will allow chemistry instructors to better understand how to scaffold their students’ development of the implicit skills associated with chemistry expertise.

articles.title: Personalizing Structured Self-Help in the Moment: Students’ Experiences With Embedded AI Chatbots in a Guided Digital Mental Health Platform
articles.authors: Sascha Y Struijs
articles.abstract:
Background: University students can use guided digital mental health interventions without having immediate access to a coach. Fixed programme content does not always answer questions about choosing a programme or applying an exercise to a personal situation. This study examined whether purpose-specific large language model chatbots can address this gap within an existing platform, MoodLift. The study focused on how students judged their usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety.
Methods: Two prototypes developed for MoodLift were evaluated: a Program Selection Assistant and an AI Coach. Ten first-year students used both tools. They completed usability and acceptability measures before joining one of two focus groups. Questionnaire results were summarized descriptively. Focus-group transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.
Results: Mean Chatbot Usability Questionnaire scores were 70.3 for the Program Selection Assistant and 70.8 for the AI Coach. Acceptability ratings were generally positive. Five themes were developed: (1) from general self-help to personal support; (2) providing direction while preserving autonomy; (3) students trusted the chatbots conditionally, not automatically; (4) embedding made AI more relevant and legitimate; and (5) safety required a bounded, complementary role. Situational fit emerged as a cross-cutting principle: preferences varied between students and depended on the task and context.
Conclusions: Purpose-specific chatbots can help students use guided digital self-help at the moment questions arise. Their value depends on reliable responses and an explicit scope. Providers should explain how data are handled and who remains responsible, while ensuring that human support is available

articles.title: From Behavioral Instructions to Perceptual Goals: Manipulating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Communication Experiments
articles.authors: Xingman Wu
articles.abstract: Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences. Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting. Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism. Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism. Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86–.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence. These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human–AI communication research.

articles.title: Toward a More Inclusive Motivation Science
articles.authors: Franki Y. H. Kung; Ziqi Yao; Zhixu (Rick) Yang; Aryca Woodson; Dante Raymond Raymond Bruno; Abigail Scholer; Amanda Diekman
articles.abstract: Good science has the power to move and change lives. At its best, motivation science not only deepens the understanding of human behavior but also contributes meaningfully to improving the lives of people and communities. Central to its excellence is the field’s capacity to speak to a broad spectrum of contexts and human experiences. In this chapter, we reflected on the current state of motivation science by discussing its historical emphasis on universality and considering how greater attention to specificity can further advance the field. We then outlined three promising directions for future development and offer recommendations to support sustainable and systemic change. By moving toward a more inclusive motivation science, we hope to enhance both the field’s knowledge and its community, strengthening a discipline that more accurately reflects and effectively serves the diverse populations it aims to understand.

articles.title: Expertise Shapes the Multidimensional Perception of Stories
articles.authors: Qingzhi Ruby Zeng; Derek Lilienthal; Coraline Rinn Iordan; Aaron Steven White; Elise A. Piazza
articles.abstract: Storytelling is a primary means of human connection and creative expression, but it is unclear how mechanisms of story perception may vary across people with differing expertise. Here, we examined how expertise in creative storytelling shapes ratings of five dimensions of story quality (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness), as well as how these ratings are influenced by four linguistic feature categories (language productivity, lexical predictability, semantic similarity, and lexical composition). Online storytellers (N=18) improvised six spoken stories each (for a total of 108 stories). The transcript of each story was rated by both novices (N=10-31) and creative writing/storytelling experts (N=15) on the five story dimensions and analyzed using the four linguistic feature categories above. Overall, experts and novices provided similar average ratings, and their rating spaces both showed two distinct underlying principal components–essentially, creativity and cohesiveness–which were, in turn, predicted by distinct linguistic features. However, experts perceived the five dimensions as more differentiated, and their ratings were less driven by linguistic features than novices’. These findings indicate that experts’ judgments are more nuanced but also may rely less on fine-grained structural features of narratives, highlighting the importance of capturing individual differences and multidimensionality in story perception.

articles.title: Introducing ResIN: An Applied Tutorial to the Response-Item-Networks Package for R
articles.authors: Philip Warncke; Dino Carpentras; Adrian Lueders; Michael Quayle
articles.abstract: We introduce ResIN, a package for the R programming language designed to estimate, visualize, and analyze Response-Item Networks (ResIN ). ResIN is an increasingly popular method for modeling complex socio-political attitude systems as sparse, spatially interpretable networks. The package simplifies and unifies the underlying workflow while offering a range of convenience features, including network plotting, community detection, psychometric score extraction, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, and the export of ResIN objects to other statistical software environments. We provide an overview of the ResIN method, its computational implementation in R, and demonstrate the utility of key package features through an applied replication tutorial based on a recent study by Lüders et al., 2024

articles.title: Literacy Skills are Related to Audiovisual Speech Perception in School-Aged Children
articles.authors: Shakhlo Nematova; Sarah Akkad; Henry Brice; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles.abstract: Does learning to read influence children’s audiovisual (AV) speech perception? This study aimed to answer this question by delving into whether the process of learning to read in Uzbek, a language with a transparent orthography, influences the sensitivity to AV speech cues (i.e., mouth movements corresponding to phonetic/lexical information). Furthermore, the study examined the mediating role of phonological awareness (PA) skills in potentially linking reading and AV speech sensitivity. 283 pre-readers (age=5-6 years) and readers (age=7-10 years) in Tashkent, Uzbekistan completed PA, AV speech perception, and reading assessments. Overall, better reading skills predicted increased sensitivity to AV speech cues. These findings suggest that there is a potential shared mechanism between reading and AV speech perception. However, in the case of languages with transparent orthographies, this shared mechanism does not seem to be significantly mediated by phonological awareness skills of children.

articles.title: Modifiable Psychological Variables as Predictors of Return to Work: Temporal Patterns in a Longitudinal Observational Study
articles.authors: Magnus Johansson; Alice Giöstad; Aleksandra Bujacz; Anna Ek; Petter Gustavsson; Lars-Göran Öst; Anna Finnes
articles.abstract:
Background: Common mental disorders (CMDs), including depression, anxiety, and adjustment disorders, are leading causes of long-term sickness absence (SA) and work disability in high-income countries. Despite the significant burden, evidence-based interventions to support return to work (RTW) remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the predictive role of selected modifiable psychological factors on RTW among individuals on sick leave for CMDs, with particular emphasis on temporal dynamics during the early phase of the RTW process. 

Methods: A longitudinal observational study was conducted with bi-weekly self-reported questionnaire measurements for 3 months and quarterly follow-ups for 12 months. Outcomes were self-reported RTW and registry-based net SA days (NSAD). Analyses included robust linear mixed models for focal predictor trajectories, Bayesian logistic regression with a regularizing horseshoe prior for the probability of RTW, and ordered beta regression for NSAD since sick-days data have lower and upper bounds. 

Results: Baseline measurements of RTW-SE and Work Ability Scores (WAS) were also associated with RTW at three months. Improvement in RTW self-efficacy (RTW-SE) during the first three months showed the strongest and most consistent association with increased probability of RTW, both cross-sectionally at 3, 6, and 12 months, and longitudinally.  

Improvement regarding physical fatigue and WAS were associated with approximately 18% less NSAD at 3 and 6 months, while cognitive exhaustion showed similar impact but only at three months.

articles.title: Patterns of Reactivity in Misophonia: Profiles of Behavioral and Self-Reported Symptoms
articles.authors: Nico Remmert; Mercedes Woolley; Marta Siepsiak; Michael Twohig; Steffi Pohl
articles.abstract: Individuals with misophonia experience intense affective reactions to trigger sounds and often cope through avoidance. Avoidance may be anticipatory (preventing exposure) or reactive (escaping exposure), but individual patterns remain poorly understood. In a sample of individuals with misophonia (N = 370), we used Gaussian mixture modeling to identify profiles based on anticipatory avoidance, reactive escape, and emotional responses. We compared profiles derived from behavioral assessments and self-reports and examined their associations with clinical outcomes. Behavioral data revealed three qualitatively distinct profiles: high affective reactivity, anticipatory-dominant reactivity, and reactive-dominant reactivity. Self-reports instead yielded four profiles that mainly reflected severity differences. Agreement between methods was modest, suggesting that they capture partly different aspects of misophonic responding. Behavioral profiles also differed in clinically relevant outcomes. These findings highlight the value of behavioral assessment for identifying distinct response styles and advancing understanding of misophonia beyond symptom severity.

articles.title: The Museum as a Spatial System: Bodily Movement, Visual Comparison and Memory in Art Viewing
articles.authors: Anna Miscenà; Xingyu Long; Carola Korhummel; Zoya Dare; Dijana Popovic; Corinna Kühnapfel; Jörg Helmut Mühlhans; Raphael Rosenberg
articles.abstract: Art viewing in museums inherently relies on physical movement through galleries. While research has begun to examine movement in art perception, it has focused mainly on abstract paintings and small-scale case studies. We investigated how bodily movement, gaze behaviour and memory interact with a mobile-eye-tracking study in Vienna's Leopold Museum (145 visitors viewing 66 paintings across six rooms). The results show that a) although visitors increased their viewing distance for larger paintings, they did not maintain a constant visual angle, b) visitors repositioned themselves mainly laterally in front of paintings, and c) they frequently compared neighbouring artworks by repeating gazes between paintings. Longer viewing times and repeated returns to a painting were associated with better subsequent memory. These findings suggest that the museum's "white cube" is not a neutral backdrop for independent encounters but a spatially organised environment that shapes horizontal exploration as well as visual comparison between adjacent works.

articles.title: Mouthing in comprehension of multimodal multilingual units in Norwegian Sign Language
articles.authors: Felicia Bisnath; Maren Sørhaug; Benjamin Anible
articles.abstract: Mouthings -- mouth movements that mimic spoken language words produced alongside signing -- are a unique multimodal phenomenon in that they recruit resources from a second language; however, they have not received much attention in research that explicitly frames itself as multimodal. In Norwegian Sign Language (NSL/NTS), the role of mouthing in comprehension has not been studied extensively from the perspective of deaf users of the language. In this study, we add to these two understudied areas by exploring mouthings in comprehension of Norwegian Sign Language in an unrestricted lexical identification paradigm (N=30). We find that when manual forms are polysemous, plausible mouthings improve accuracy in lexical identification and the certainty of comprehension. When mouthings are implausible, it appears that the dominant strategy is to make identification decisions based on the manual form only. In a smaller number of cases participants appeared to rely solely on the mouthing or blended the mouthing and manual components.

articles.title: Cognitive Model Organism: The Unboxing of Thinking Process
articles.authors: Yuncheng Jia; Bo Qin; Anuchit Phanumartwiwath
articles.abstract: We establish the Hortus Regis Alti (HRA) Experimental and Observational Protocol for studying a frozen language model as a cognitive model organism. The preparation combines controlled input perturbations, complete native-token preservation, deterministic symbolic probes, contextual process coding, and explicit failure screening. One DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B implementation with INT8 linear layers and BF16 elsewhere produced 176 archived trajectories across four observation configurations of one Bayesian decision problem, containing 2,205,963 generated tokens. Eight baseline pairs regenerated identical overlapping prefixes across 93,016 token positions. Three empirical demonstrations organize the study. Symbolic closure separated from execution termination, including renewed processing after a closure marker. Aggregate consumption separated from item-specific response paths: 36 of 40 four-level item series changed direction. Correct local computation separated from maintenance of task representation: an auxiliary result could be calculated correctly and subsequently rebound as an operand. Complete contextual reading localized 1,926 evidence anchors, including successful repairs and recurrent failures. Measurement checks further showed that a short window could classify a long exact cycle as highly diverse. These findings motivate testable hypotheses of representational control competition, training-register capture, and content-specific effects of symbolic continuation. The contribution is a process-oriented experimental preparation, a reproducible trajectory collection, and a quality-control procedure that connects observable symbolic events to discriminating intervention sites. Precision specifications identify the model strain, execution conditions, measurement units, semantic coding decisions, and regeneration range supporting these claims.

articles.title: Identifying Discrepancies Between Measurements of Visual, Felt Presence and Tactile, Judged Presence
articles.authors: Oliver Singleton; Marianna Obrist; Aikaterini Fotopoulou
articles.abstract:
Unlike other screen-based technologies such as computer monitors, virtual reality (VR)
systems allow the user to feel a sense of presence – the sense that they are actually
situated within the surrounding virtual environment. Although the foundational experience of
existing within a physical environment goes far beyond aspects of vision, our study is the
first, to our knowledge, to operationalise and measure different facets of the
multidimensional concept of the SOOP, ranging from indirect, trial-by-trial measures of
reaction times and accuracy to higher-order aspects of presence judgements such as their
trial-by-trial metacognitive efficiency, and to modality-specific and modality-general global
(i.e. across many trials), retrospective self-report measures. We primarily hypothesised that
whilst multisensory stimulation is the most important factor in the creation of presence,
unisensory touch will be a greater causative factor in the creation of presence than
unisensory vision. 44 participants completed an implicit reaction-time task (reacting to target
stimuli) and an explicit metacognitive task (rating confidence in object presence). We
manipulated sense type (unisensory vs multisensory), sensory modality (vision vs touch) and
temporal order (e.g., touch-first vs. vision-first). Results indicated that multisensory
integration significantly enhanced metacognitive efficacy, accuracy and reaction speeds
compared to unisensory conditions. However, a key dissociation emerged between
unisensory modalities. While participants reacted faster to visual stimuli, they achieved
higher perceptual accuracy with tactile stimuli, with participants retrospectively rating touch
as feeling significantly more "real" than vision. These findings support the notion that realtime "felt" presence and retrospective "judged" presence may be caused by distinct factors.

articles.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles.title: A climate policy referendum decreases pluralistic ignorance on climate change concern
articles.authors: Viktoria Cologna; Jana Freundt; Eugenia Bajet Mestre; Niels G. Mede; Lauren Christine Howe; Jamie Lee Gloor; Eri Bertsou; Naomi Oreskes; Reto Knutti; Mike S. Schäfer
articles.abstract: Pluralistic ignorance about others’ climate change concern can contribute to inaction on climate change. We conducted a two-wave panel study (Npre = 1,578, Npost = 827) with a general sample before and after the national Swiss referendum on the Climate Protection Law, which was accepted. We find that people underestimate others’ concern about climate change and others’ support of scientists’ policy advocacy. Pluralistic ignorance of climate change concern slightly decreased after the referendum, while pluralistic ignorance of scientists’ advocacy remained unchanged. Results thus show that national voting on climate policy creates a window of opportunity that can be harnessed to reduce pluralistic ignorance.

articles.title: Mapping the Body in the Brain with the Mind
articles.authors: Alexander M Puckett; Ashley York; Saskia Bollmann; Ross Cunnington
articles.abstract: Using a magnet and a mind, we revealed the brain’s somatotopic organization without touching the body. Fingertip representations were first mapped using vibrotactile stimulation at 7T, then again by directing attention across the fingers under constant vibration. Finally, attention was directed to the fingertips and facial regions using only auditory cues, without any external tactile stimulation. Prior training in a sensory-restricted float tank subjectively sharpened attentional precision and bodily awareness. Remarkably, somatotopic maps emerged in the absence of external tactile stimulation – showing that structured attention alone can reveal the brain’s somatotopic organization.

articles.title: Elected by the face? Facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal conditions predict voting intentions
articles.authors: Antonio Olivera-LaRosa; Guido Corradi; Sergio Barbosa; Sissy Delgado-Pacheco; William Jimenez-Leal; Gonzalo Luna-Cortes; Javier Villacampa; Jaume Rosselló
articles.abstract: Rapid judgments based on political candidates' facial features often predict electoral outcomes. Building on this, we explored how facial impressions of honesty and competence—formed under suboptimal processing conditions—predict voting intentions for actual political candidates. In this study, 484 participants (Colombians: 199; Peruvians: 285; male: 30.2%) were exposed to candidate faces from Colombia and Peru under time constraints (33 ms or 100 ms). Participants rated these faces on honesty and competence and subsequently indicated their likelihood of voting for each candidate. Our findings demonstrate that while rapid facial impressions predict voting preferences overall, this effect is strongly amplified when candidates are recognized from one's own country, whereas for foreign candidates, the relationship remains minimal or disappears. Crucially, because voting intentions were evaluated during subsequent unconstrained viewing, these rapid impressions interact with full-viewing processing rather than acting in complete isolation. By utilizing real candidate photographs, this study confirms that rapid facial impressions align with electoral preferences in naturalistic settings, operating through an integrated process where familiar faces instantly retrieve pre-existing political attitudes.

articles.title: Toward Sensory Accounts of Autistic Masking: A Perspective
articles.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Melanie Heyworth; Timothy Chan; Diana Weiting Tan
articles.abstract: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts. However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes. Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored. In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations. Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences. We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking. While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments. We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression. We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

articles.title: Computationally efficient interval estimation for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R: A replication of Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006)
articles.authors: Carl F. Falk; Elizabeth Savchenko
articles.abstract: Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006) developed a popular estimation approach for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, using simulations to evaluate the performance of two computationally efficient ways to obtain intervals for the indirect effect. While the model can be estimated in a variety of software packages, support in R lags behind as the original approaches to interval estimation were demonstrated using commercial software. Recent research with R instead has only demonstrated interval estimation with more computationally intensive methods. Meanwhile, other recent work has focused attention towards how Monte Carlo simulation studies are conducted and reported, highlighting the importance of replicating previous findings. Our goals in this manuscript are twofold. First, we show how to implement the original computationally efficient interval estimation methods for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R. We do so by using the Delta method to obtain elements of the asymptotic covariance matrix among model parameters necessary for these approaches. Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate the original simulation study by Bauer et al. (2006). In general, our results indicate that our implementation is operating as expected as Type I error rates and coverage were acceptable when assumptions were met. Furthermore, though we observed higher convergence rates, the major findings from Bauer et al. (2006) were replicated. We hope that extensions to this work will help lead to more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models being readily available to applied researchers.

articles.title: Learning and Using Value Maps in Multi-Dimensional Choice
articles.authors: Ata Baris Karagoz; Akram Bakkour
articles.abstract:
When making choices between multi-dimensional options, people draw upon knowledge
of the options’ various properties to make a decision. While much work has probed how
individuals make decisions in these modes, less is known of how learned value maps can
be flexibly composed to support novel decisions. Here we taught participants three separate
perceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five value
categories. We then had them choose between composite options never encountered during
learning while a mouse-contingent display forced serial information sampling. How the learned
map was read during choice varied widely across people, from fully metric reads (e.g. how
much better) to purely ordinal ones (e.g. which is ahead). We find that ordinal comparison is
not simply a degraded version of the same metric. Instead, participants mix between ordinal
and metric reads. How well each dimension was learned set its weight, while how strongly
learning accuracy depended on the separation between categories lowered both the weights
and the metric share of the read. Both the readout and weights left separable signatures in
information search. Learned value maps are thus composed and then read out to guide choice.

articles.title: Team Science: An Examination of Factors Associated with Citation Metrics
articles.authors: Kelly Cuccolo; Jordan Rose Wagge; John Edlund; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Scientific collaboration, often measured through co-authorship, has grown in many disciplines and is frequently linked to increased citation rates. However, it remains unclear which disciplines have seen the greatest growth in collaboration and how this growth relates to article-level metrics. Moreover, little is known about how team demographics (e.g., h-index, gender, number of institutions) and team size interact with regard to research impact. Understanding these dynamics is essential given their influence on hiring, tenure, and the broader scientific ecosystem. Using metadata from Elsevier’s International Center for the Study of Research (ICSR) Lab, we examined collaboration trends across disciplines and their associations with citation outcomes. Team size increased over time, with variation by discipline, and was positively associated with citation counts. Gender relationships with citation rates varied by authorship order and discipline, indicating a complex relationship between gender and impact. Greater institutional and geographic diversity were linked to higher citation counts. Last authors’ h-indices were especially strongly associated with impact, particularly when self-citations were excluded. Effect sizes were small, and the observational design precludes causal conclusions. These findings describe how evolving patterns of collaboration are related to research visibility and underscore the importance of considering team composition, cautiously, in evaluations of scientific output.

articles.title: The Culture of Dissemblance Among Black American Women: A Mixed Methods Assessment
articles.authors: Linzie Taylor; Natalie Merril; Trinidi Prochaska; Amanda R. Arnold; Amy R Murphy; Megan E. Huibregtse; Angela Li; Abigail Powers; Vasiliki Michopoulos; Jennifer Stevens
articles.abstract: Disparities in the treatment of mood and stress disorders like posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may partially reflect a limited culturally informed understanding of emotional processing. The culture of dissemblance (COD) describes how American Black women learned to mask their emotional expression as a protective mechanism within a society that places them at greater risk of psychosocial stressors while invalidating their emotional experience. This mixed methods study examined COD among forty-nine Black women (ages 40–55), who completed a semi-structured interview assessing emotional engagement alongside self-report measures of emotion regulation, trauma exposure, PTSD symptoms, racial discrimination, and Black identity. Thematic analysis indicated that participants experienced negative judgments of their emotional expression and learned to monitor emotional responses for self-protection. 83.7% of women reported less emotional expression in public with 40.8% of women identified the workplace as the primary site for emotional masking. Interview-based COD endorsement associated with belief in negative public perception of Black people but not with the other variables of interests. Treatment approaches should center Black women's cultural knowledge to address mental health disparities.

articles.title: Commitment-Driven Information Seeking in Misinformation Consumption
articles.authors: Alessandro Miani; Théo Schöpfer; Stephan Lewandowsky; Thomas Hills; Adrian Bangerter
articles.abstract: The role of social media in misinformation consumption remains contested. This disagreement might arise from the failure to distinguish incidental exposure to misinformation from deliberate consumption. We address this gap by analyzing incoming traffic data, collected in November 2020, to more than 2,000 websites that vary in misinformation and type of bias (liberal, conservative, and conspiracy). We compare the traffic modalities through which users reach those sites: direct traffic, such as typing a URL or using a bookmark (mostly associated with self-directed information seeking); social traffic, from links clicked on social media; and search traffic, from search engines (mostly associated with incidental exposure). We found that reliable, low-misinformation websites are reached mainly via search traffic, whereas unreliable ones are mostly reached via direct traffic; this pattern is stronger for conspiracy websites. Breaking down social traffic by platform reveals that Facebook was the main driver of traffic towards unreliable websites, mostly towards politically biased and entry-level conspiracy websites. These findings suggest that structural interventions such as algorithmic adjustments and content moderation may reduce incidental exposure among users with low belief commitment, but are unlikely to deter highly committed information seekers, who require targeted, ideologically informed strategies.

articles.title: Is a joke funnier if it is told by a man? A novel paradigm using AI-generated voices
articles.authors: Amy Zhao
articles.abstract: The stereotype that “men are funnier than women” is culturally pervasive. In a large preregistered online study (n=966), participants rated 12 jokes delivered by a male or female AI-generated voice. To control for differences in delivery, cadence, and intonation, we used a speech-to-speech transformation to transform jokes spoken by a female into a male version and vice versa. Using a Bayesian analysis, we found strong evidence that the apparent gender of the speaker does not affect the perceived funniness of the joke (BF=0.023). We found no interaction between the original and apparent voice gender on masculinity ratings, indicating that vocal gender cues were effectively eliminated when voices were transformed to the opposite gender, reinforcing the merit of this gender manipulation method. Further, men had significantly higher agreement that being funny is a masculine trait than women (MD=0.73, padj<.001), and participants with more male than female friends had significantly higher agreement with this belief than those with equal numbers of male and female friends (MD=0.68, padj<.001) or more female than male friends (MD=0.91, padj<.001). In all, apparent vocal gender does not appear to influence humour evaluations directly, but exploratory findings suggest the apparent vocal gender and delivery may shape broader impressions of speakers (such as perceived confidence and charisma). And individual differences such as gender and proportion of male friends may shape gendered attitudes and expectations toward humour.

articles.title: Bayesian posterior predictive checks for person-fit analysis: A comparison of approaches illustrated with the lz* statistic
articles.authors: Jorge Tendeiro
articles.abstract: Person-fit analysis is a popular framework in item response theory aimed at flagging observed response patterns that substantially deviate from a fitted model’s predictions. In this paper we combine and extend previous work by comparing alternative implementations of Bayesian posterior predictive checks for person-fit analysis. Two of the implementations adapt proposals by Berkhof et al. (2004) to person fit for the first time. The suggested procedures are generic and may be used with any person-fit statistic; we use the lz* statistic for illustration purposes. Data-driven empirically calibrated thresholds to use for flagging aberrant response patterns are derived as part of the methodology. Through two simulation studies, we identify two of the considered approaches that generally performed best across varying scenarios of response misfit, one semi-Bayesian and the other fully Bayesian. Our simulations further show that the calibrated thresholds for some approaches differ substantially from their nominal threshold counterparts. We illustrate how to use these procedures by means of an empirical example. Our results offer concrete guidance for practitioners conducting person-fit analysis within the Bayesian framework.

articles.title: Respiratory Phase and Visuospatial Attention: A Replication and Extension
articles.authors: Timothy Ethan Roberts; Bethanie Richards; Paul Anthony Skarratt; Martin Fischer; Shane Lindsay
articles.abstract: Recent studies suggest that respiration may influence visuospatial processing. In two experiments, Belli and Fischer (2024) reported faster detection of targets on the right at inhalation peaks and targets on the left at exhalation troughs. We sought to replicate those findings and to test whether the influence of breathing phase on spatial responding would also extend to the vertical dimension. Experiment 1 used a visual probe detection task and Experiment 2 used an exogenous Posner cueing task. Targets appeared at horizontal and vertical locations, with trials manually triggered at visually identified inhalation peaks and exhalation troughs. Across both experiments, the predicted spatial pattern did not emerge on either axis. Experiment 1 yielded no reliable phase effect, whereas Experiment 2 showed shorter reaction times in the inhalation condition than in the exhalation condition across target locations, consistent with a general change in response speed associated with inhalation.

articles.title: The conflicted student and the internal battle over generative AI use
articles.authors: Stephen Harrison Dewitt; Metodi Siromahov; Duncan Brumby; Silvia Bodei
articles.abstract: The common narrative around university students and generative AI is one of crisis. Underpinning this is an implicit assumption: if students have the capacity to cheat, they will. Our survey reveals two missing factors from that narrative: students have ethical principles, and students want to learn. While a minority of students might fit that implicit assumption of the crisis narrative, a similar proportion refuse to use any genAI tools at all. In between these are the majority: students using genAI tools in what they self-define as a ‘supportive’ way. These students, finding these tools unavoidable, worrying about being disadvantaged or simply finding them valuable, struggle to use them in a way that doesn’t compromise their personal sense of authorship, fits with their environmental and social principles, and doesn’t detract from their ability to learn. Students typically care greatly about these issues and are internally conflicted about this, feeling guilt when using these tools and personally trying to find that invisible line where support becomes cheating. They also use a range of rhetorical techniques to frame their personal usage and preserve their sense of authorship. We argue that we need to work with students, using approaches that enhance these feelings and encourage self-discipline, rather than primarily adopting a ‘criminal’ model of checks, detection and punishment.

articles.title: Source selection shapes the strength of cultural transmission pathways
articles.authors: Sherilyn Segura; Wouter van den Bos; Andrea Gradassi; Esra Cemre Su de Groot; Lucia Hendrikse; Lieke Hofmans; Fleur Francien Adrienne Korzilius; Sheina Lew-Levy; Ana da Silva Pinho; Scarlett Slagter
articles.abstract: Human culture depends on people learning from one another. Cultural evolutionary theory distinguishes three transmission pathways: learning from parents (vertical), non-parental adults (oblique), and peers (horizontal), which differ in how rapidly information spreads within and across generations. During middle childhood, children's social worlds expand beyond the family, creating opportunities for all three pathways to operate simultaneously, yet their relative strength has rarely been compared directly. Using 1,262 dyads of 6-13 year-olds and their parents, we examined the relative strength of vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission in two complementary behavioral experiments. Participants either received information from, or chose between, their own parent or child, an unrelated adult or child, and a peer while completing an estimation task. This design allowed us to separate two components of cultural transmission: whom people choose to learn from and how strongly they use information once it has been acquired. Vertical transmission emerged as the strongest pathway. This advantage was driven primarily by source selection, as children and parents overwhelmingly selected one another as information sources, with parents learning from their own child providing evidence for reverse vertical transmission. Once information had been acquired, however, information weighting differed little between vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission. Instead, developmental differences dominated: social information use declined markedly across middle childhood and remained consistently higher in children than in parents. Together, these findings suggest that the relative strength of cultural transmission pathways is determined primarily by source selection rather than information weighting.

articles.title: Nine-Year Changes in Work Satisfaction in Midlife – the Role of Age and Flexible Goal Adjustment
articles.authors: Georg Henning; Nadiya Kelle; Frank J Infurna
articles.abstract: As the work force is ageing and many countries raise or abolish retirement ages, it becomes more and more important to understand how work satisfaction develops over the lifespan, particularly in midlife and older age. Although many studies report positive associations of age and work satisfaction, there are only few longitudinal studies with large samples investigating within-person change over longer time spans. To overcome these limitations, we used data from the German Ageing Survey to investigate changes in work satisfaction among n = 2,588 individuals aged 40 – 59 at four measurement occasions between 2008 and 2017. As our study was informed by life span approaches to self-regulation at work, we were also interested in the role of age and flexible goal adjustment, which is the ability to adjust one’s goals according to restrictions in the environment. Results showed that work satisfaction was characterized by stability in midlife, but workers in their 60’s experienced increases in work satisfaction. Nevertheless, these effects may partly show selection effects due to dissatisfied older workers retiring over time and / or dropping out of the survey. Flexible goal adjustment was related to higher work satisfaction, but not to changes in work satisfaction. Our results demonstrate that work satisfaction can increase in older age and that flexible goal adjustment may play a role in shaping the course of work satisfaction in midlife and older age. More research is needed to understand which coping mechanisms help aging workers to stay satisfied at work.

articles.title: Whisper automatic speech recognition and humans are similarly sensitive to accents, but use sentence context differently
articles.authors: Junrong Chen; Jan Kwong; Sarah Paull; Sarah Creel
articles.abstract: Despite advancements in speech recognition technology, questions remain about model generalizability and how much models mirror human comprehension. These questions are addressed by comparing OpenAI's Whisper model and 75 human transcribers on 300 English sentences (20 speakers, half F, half M, half US-accented, half Spanish-accented). Sentences ended in 100 target words: 1⁄3 high-predictability sentences (The farmer milked the cows), 1⁄3 low- predictability (The farmer milked the nose), and 1⁄3 low-predictability+nonword (The marmer milked the nose). Target word transcription error rates were examined both in sentences and in isolation (recordings excised from same sentences). Errors decreased with increasing model size, but remained heightened for Spanish-accented vs. US-accented speech, roughly similar to human transcribers. Both models and humans benefited from higher sentence predictability. However, sentence context affected models and humans differently: humans benefited only from high- predictability sentences, while models benefited from any sentence context. Humans numerically outperformed the (best-performing) large model on isolated words and showed different error patterns, suggesting Whisper may have a restricted distribution of short utterances or may need lengthier acoustic context than humans. More varied training data and better context awareness, including speaker identity and pragmatic context, might improve ASR generalization.

articles.title: Types of Truth: How Perceived & Objective Truth Guide Belief Change
articles.authors: Keith Ransom; Bradley Walker; Piers Howe; Andrew Perfors; Yoshihisa Kashima; Nicolas Fay
articles.abstract: People must navigate socially transmitted information that varies from accurate to misleading or false.  Here, we examined how perceived and objective truth predict belief change across three studies.  In Study 1, four web-enabled frontier large language models (LLMs) and 200 human raters evaluated claims from two fact-checked datasets.  LLMs outperformed humans in inter-rater agreement and discriminative sensitivity, supporting their use as a scalable proxy for objective truth.  In Study 2 and 3, we applied this proxy to two large message corpora and examined its association with belief change.  Perceived truth and LLM-derived objective truth independently predicted belief change.  Moreover, objective truth moderated the association between perceived truth and belief change: the association between perceived truth and belief change was strongest for messages with lower objective truth and weakened as objective truth increased. These findings suggest that belief change reflects both subjective truth evaluations and the correspondence of information with reality.

articles.title: The Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS):  A Standardized 800-Picture Database for Cuteness and Kawaii Study
articles.authors: Hiroshi Nittono; Nonoka Nakamura
articles.abstract: Psychological and neuroscientific research on emotions requires publicly available stimulus materials with normative ratings. However, the necessary rating values for certain dimensions may be lacking when conducting research for specific purposes. In this study, we developed a new affective picture collection, the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS, pronounced ay-apps), intended for use in research on cuteness or kawaii in Japanese and on human–animal relationships. While cuteness is considered a stimulus attribute with positive valence, kawaii also refers to the feeling people experience when perceiving cuteness. A total of 800 animal images in the public domain or licensed under CC0 (1,000 x 1,000 pixels) were rated by 914 Japanese adults on a 9-point scale for four dimensions: valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach–avoidance), and cuteness/kawaii. Each image was rated by an average of 57 participants. Cuteness ratings were highly correlated with both valence and motivational direction (rs = .97), and the positive correlation remained moderate even when one variable was partialed out (rs = .62 and .64, respectively). These results support the idea that kawaii is a positive emotion associated with approach motivation. The AAPS images, mean rating values, and raw data are freely available for download.

articles.title: Do I experience anxiety, anger, and happiness in the same way as you do? A relational approach to emotion qualia across levels of alexithymia
articles.authors: Lin Lipeng; Zhang Chuyin; Naotsugu Tsuchiya
articles.abstract: Do people experience emotions in the same way? How can we characterize the sameness of emotional quality? Qualitative aspects of emotional experience are usually communicated through words. However, words can be ambiguous and can mean different things to different people. Here, we introduce a relational approach, which minimizes the reliance on language yet characterizes emotional experiences as structure, based on similarity judgments among emotion-evoking videos. This Registered Report will apply this method to characterize a psychological condition of “alexithymia,” which is described as “no words for emotions”. In two experiments, participants will rate the similarity between successive videos, based on the feelings evoked by the videos. Repeated video pairs will measure the degree of consistency in their similarity judgments. We will test whether individuals scoring high and low in alexithymia differ in the structure and consistency of their judgments. To disentangle the structures driven by sensory, rather than emotional, aspects of the videos, we will run a control experiment where participants rate the similarity of videos, ignoring the evoked emotions. A pilot study (N = 679) supports the feasibility of this design. By bypassing verbal reports, our approach can inform the study of emotional experience and help to clarify the nature of alexithymia.

articles.title: How Does Chatbot Anthropomorphism Shape Psychological Reactance? An Experiment on Trust and Perceived Persuasive Intent in Vaping Cessation Conversations
articles.authors: Xingman Wu
articles.abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly used to deliver health information and persuasive interventions, yet the consequences of making these systems appear humanlike remain unclear. Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors and Media Are Social Actors paradigms, mind perception theory, and psychological reactance theory, this research examined whether anthropomorphism in AI chatbots shapes reactance through two competing pathways: trust in the chatbot and perceived persuasive intent. An online between-subjects experiment was conducted among U.S. adults who currently used e-cigarettes. Participants in the main study (N = 586) were randomly assigned to interact with either an anthropomorphic or a non-anthropomorphic AI chatbot, or to view a static vaping cessation message. The results showed that interacting with an anthropomorphized chatbot reduced reactance compared to reading a static message, although this advantage did not extend to attitudes toward vaping or intentions to quit. Additionally, while anthropomorphism can generally reduce psychological reactance, its two dimensions, mindful and mindless anthropomorphism, operated in different paths. Mindful anthropomorphism was associated with greater trust and, indirectly, lower reactance. Mindless anthropomorphism was directly associated with lower reactance. These findings support the potential use of anthropomorphic AI chatbots as a communication approach for vaping cessation. Furthermore, by distinguishing mindful from mindless anthropomorphism and clarifying their distinct mechanisms, this research offers a more nuanced explanation of how humanlike AI cues shape psychological reactance and provides practical guidance for designing AI-mediated health interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Effectiveness of Stepped Care Psychological Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca A. Simonsmeier; Maren Rogawski; Elena von Wirth
articles_hidden.abstract: Stepped care has been proposed as an efficient and scalable framework for delivering pediatric psychotherapy. This meta-analysis examined the effectiveness, generalizability, and implementation characteristics of stepped care interventions for the prevention and treatment of mental health problems in children and adolescents. Across included studies, stepped care interventions demonstrated large significant overall pre–post improvements in health outcomes (d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.944; 1.50]). When compared with control conditions effects were small and non-significant (d = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.133; 0.313]) suggesting that stepped care yields outcomes comparable to standard care including intensive treatments rather than superior clinical effects. Moderator analyses indicated that stepped care effects were largely consistent across patient characteristics, outcomes and methodological qualities. Importantly, stepped care interventions were associated with significantly lower costs compared to control conditions, highlighting their economic advantage. Most studies combined relatively intensive steps, with limited use of self-directed, low-intensity, scalable interventions as initial treatment components. Stepping decisions were primarily based on disorder-specific symptom measures, although some studies incorporated shared decision-making involving clinicians, patients, and families. Exploratory analyses revealed that approximately 46% of the patients transitioned from the initial step, independent of age, and timing of the decision point. Overall, outcomes of stepped care in pediatric psychotherapy appear clinically comparable to usual care while offering substantial cost benefits. The findings support its promise as an efficient service delivery model while underscoring the need for further research on potential barriers and optimal implementation strategies in clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: An Elaborated Model of Youth Externalizing Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Irwin Waldman; Holly E Poore
articles_hidden.abstract: Externalizing is an integral spectrum in hierarchical dimensional models of psychopathology. Comprehensive models of Externalizing have been developed for late adolescents and adults, but not for youth. We developed and characterized an elaborated model of youth Externalizing psychopathology using item response theory and confirmatory factor analyses of ADHD, ODD, and CD symptoms to investigate the psychometric properties of Externalizing’s components. Participants included large population-representative twin and clinic-referred samples of youth. Using several criteria, increasingly elaborated models comprising an Externalizing dimension and seven fine-grained symptom factors outperformed models containing omnibus ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom dimensions. Results replicated across clinic and twin samples, with the Externalizing dimension most strongly reflecting defiant behavior. Symptom domains varied in their measurement properties across levels of Externalizing. This elaborated model of youth Externalizing sets the stage for future investigations of causes and outcomes, and for examining measurement invariance across individuals of diverse backgrounds.

articles_hidden.title: Crowdstorming You Can Trust? Assessing the Reliability of Crowdsourced Ideation and Prioritization
articles_hidden.authors: Younes JEDDI; Maurice Balick; Emile Servan-Schreiber
articles_hidden.abstract: Asking crowds of stakeholders to generate and prioritize ideas has become commonplace, from citizen assemblies to corporate open-innovation challenges. Although the reliability of the results of such consultations is taken for granted, their consistency across independent groups has received little empirical attention, largely because such processes are typically one-off events that cannot easily be repeated. In this exploratory study, we introduce the concept of parallel-crowds reliability, the consistency of outcomes when the same collective intelligence process is applied to the same problem by different but demographically equivalent crowds, and we provide an initial empirical test of it. Two separate but equivalent groups of MBA students in the same course were asked to independently propose and prioritize ideas to improve their MBA program, with the same decision-maker curating and selecting winning ideas in both groups. We assess reliability at three successive stages using semantic similarity measures based on two independent embedding models. We find that the two groups independently proposed semantically similar ideas, with convergence concentrated among valuable ideas and divergence among poor ones. They also prioritized similar ideas similarly, enabling the decision maker to select similar sets of winning ideas. Given the single-domain design, we frame these results as an initial evidence base for future investigations.

articles_hidden.title: Cannabis Use and Binge Eating in Emerging Adults: High Prevalence and High Burden Across Ten Years of the Healthy Minds Study
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Lingxiao Liu; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Existing evidence on co-occurring binge eating and cannabis use is preliminary, and it is unclear how common the combination is or how much burden it carries. We examined both questions among college students, who are high risk for both behaviors.

Method: We pooled ten annual cohorts (2015–16 to 2024–25) of the Healthy Minds Study (577,962 students, 807 campus-year clusters). Eating pathology was measured with the SCOFF loss-of-control item. A subsample of 17,114 students also completed the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Estimates were weighted for non-response and clustered by campus.

Results: Across cohorts, loss of control over eating was reported by 39.0% of past-30-day cannabis users and 30.7% of non-users (adjusted OR = 1.43, p < .001). Severe SCOFF screening (score of 4 or higher) rose from 3.5% in non-users to 7.1% in near-daily users (adjusted OR per step = 1.22, p < .001). Weekly binge eating (EDE-Q) was more common among users (23.4% vs. 15.3%; adjusted OR = 1.68, p < .001). Overall, 8.3% of all students reported both behaviors. Students reporting both had higher odds of 10 out of 11 correlates. Relative excess risk due to the interaction between cannabis use and loss of control over eating was positive for depression, self-injury, suicidal ideation, and academic harm (odds ratio based; p < .001).

Conclusions: Binge eating is common among students who use cannabis and is more severe at higher frequencies of cannabis use. Importantly, co-occurrence carried higher odds of depression, suicidality, self-injury, and academic harm. Thus, these cross-sectional findings underscore the need for dedicated longitudinal research.

articles_hidden.title: Appreciating Ambiguity in Art: The effects of semantic distance and insight confidence on aesthetic appreciation
articles_hidden.authors: Rajat Ravi Rao; manon mulckhuyse; Michiel van Elk; Francesco Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous work in psychology of aesthetics suggests that people tend to appreciate artworks they subjectively perceive as ambiguous. Yet ambiguity of an artwork is typically measured through viewers’ own ratings or qualitative measures which are well suited to within-person questions, but they do not, on their own, describe how much viewers disagree about what a work means. Defining ambiguity as the degree to which an artwork affords multiple interpretations, we introduce a computational, description-based measure that quantifies this multiplicity as the semantic distance between viewers’ descriptions. We complemented this with a metacognitive measure, insight confidence, which captures how confident viewers are in their own interpretations. We examined how these measures relate to aesthetic appreciation, operationalised as interest, emotional intensity, and cognitive affect. In an online study (N = 123), participants viewed artworks for 6 seconds and for each individual artwork either described them, rated their insight confidence and provided cognitive affect ratings, or they provided interest and emotional intensity ratings.  Across artworks, those eliciting more divergent descriptions (greater semantic distance) received lower mean insight confidence. Contrary to preregistered predictions, such artworks also received lower aesthetic appreciation. These results indicate aesthetic appreciation is more strongly related to how certain a viewer is about what they are viewing rather than the degree of ambiguity of an artwork. Methodologically, the approach offers a way to quantify the divergence of open-ended verbal interpretations across viewers, alongside a measure of viewers' confidence in their own interpretation.

articles_hidden.title: Transdiagnostic factors differentially shape choices and reaction times in social evaluative learning
articles_hidden.authors: Aamir Sohail; Aleksandra Magda; Muna Said; Laura Phillips; Yifei Lu; Georgina Reynolds; Alice Comer-Fenn; Jessie Russell; Huafeng Lu; Tally Sims
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories. 

Methods
Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas ‘liked,’ ‘disliked,’ or were ‘neutral’ toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits. 

Results
Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed faster reaction times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valanced conditions and was associated with faster reaction times overall. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms. 

Conclusions
These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

articles_hidden.title: Characterizing Rejection Sensitivity in Autistic Adolescents and Implications for Depression and Anxiety Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Elika Parab; Colleen Sbeglia; Vana Matevosian; Pia Hernandez; Jessica Schwartzman
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is a developmental period characterized by increased interest in peer relationships and social inclusion. Rejection sensitivity (RS) – the tendency to anticipate, perceive, and experience heightened emotional responses to rejection – is common in adolescence and linked to internalizing symptoms. However, RS is understudied in autistic adolescents despite their social communication differences, increased risk of peer rejection, and online lived experiences of heightened rejection sensitivity. It is also unknown how RS impacts different mental health symptoms and whether it might contribute to the heightened prevalence of anxiety and depression in autistic youth. In the present study, 106 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) completed surveys of RS, internalizing symptoms, autistic traits, self-esteem, and peer victimization. Results showed that virtually all autistic adolescents experienced a degree of RS, with higher rates among females and those with higher autistic traits. Hierarchical regression models indicated that Anxious RS predicted social anxiety symptoms above and beyond traditional risk and protective factors, but neither Anxious nor Angry RS predicted depression or generalized anxiety. Findings have implications for risk stratification models and point to potential intervention targets; yet more research is needed to determine the directionality of relationships with rejection sensitivity.

articles_hidden.title: Does Daily Meditation Increase Self-Compassion? A Bayesian Multilevel Diary Study
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Monnot
articles_hidden.abstract:
Evaluations of brief self-compassion programs usually compare phases, leaving open whether 
meditation and nonmeditation days differ. With few nonmeditation days, subtracting each 
person's observed average can distort the separation of day-level from person-level effects. This 
secondary analysis used the archival 28-day diary of 65 employees in a two-week online self
compassion meditation program, with morning reports of meditation over the previous 24 hours 
(Li et al., 2021). Across 14 intervention days, a prespecified Bayesian two-level model treated 
each person's meditation propensity as latent, separating the within-person contrast between 
meditation and nonmeditation days from stable differences in meditation frequency. Hypotheses 
were higher same-day self-compassion on meditation days (primary) and lower next-day 
emotional exhaustion, adjusting for same-day exhaustion (secondary). Results are posterior 
medians, 95% credible intervals (CrIs), and directional probabilities. For same-day self
compassion, the meditation-day slope had median = 0.00 SD, 95% CrI [−0.09, 0.09], P(b > 0) = 
.48; for next-day exhaustion, the slope had median = −0.03 SD, 95% CrI [−0.16, 0.11], P(b < 0) 
= .65. Both CrIs spanned zero. An archival intervention diary can answer an adherence question 
its original phase-based analysis did not ask.

articles_hidden.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
articles_hidden.authors: Caitlin Lloyd; Zarrar Shehzad; Janet Schebendach; Akram Bakkour; Alice M Xue; Naomi Assaf; Rayman Jiliani; B. Timothy Walsh; Daphna Shohamy; Joanna Steinglass
articles_hidden.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Diary Study of Sexual and Gender Minority Emerging Adults’ Stressors:  Codesign and Preliminary Findings
articles_hidden.authors: Noah J French; Margaret Atkinson-Barnes; Tanvi Lakhtakia; Emma C. Wolfe; Md. Sabbir Ahmed; Laura Barnes; Bethany Teachman
articles_hidden.abstract: Emerging adulthood involves impactful developmental milestones for sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals and is a critical period for understanding stress processes. Most existing SGM stress research is cross-sectional, with relatively little known about the everyday experiences that may confer mental health risk or resilience for SGM emerging adults. N = 104 SGM emerging adults (age: M = 20.21 years, SD = 1.92 years; 76% assigned female at birth; 35% gender minority; 53% Bisexual+; 55% White) were recruited to codesign (Phases 1-2) or complete for 14 days (Phase 3) a daily diary measure of identity-related and non-identity-related stressors and positive identity-related experiences. Phase 1 participants (n = 8) completed qualitative interviews and provided feedback on an initial draft measure. Phase 2 participants (n = 6) piloted a revised measure for seven days before providing feedback in qualitative interviews. Phase 3 participants (n = 90) completed the final measure for 14 days. Qualitative data from Phases 1-2 were analyzed using the immersion-crystallization framework, and descriptive statistics were computed for Phase 3 quantitative data. In Phases 1-2, participants emphasized the need to capture chronic stressors and stress tied to recent sociopolitical events in the U.S. In Phase 3, non-identity-related stressors were more frequent than identity-related stressors, proximal identity-related stressors were more frequent than distal identity-related stressors, and negative intersectional experiences and positive identity-related experiences were both common. Results highlight the importance of involving participants with lived experiences in all stages of survey design.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Reported Precipitants of Psychosis, Mania, and Depression: An AI-Assisted Analysis of Reddit
articles_hidden.authors: Ari Brouwer; Charles L Raison
articles_hidden.abstract: We examined self-reported precipitants of mania, psychosis, and depression on Reddit using AI-assisted code development and automated coding, with blinded human validation. Analyses compared precipitants of mania (n = 337), psychosis (n = 339), and depression (n = 252). Generic stress and sleep disruption were common to mania and psychosis but rare in depression. Cannabis and trauma/abuse/assault were more frequently reported for psychosis, while antidepressants and positive activation/reward were more frequently reported for mania, and self-evaluative thought patterns and social isolation/rejection for depression. Automated and human coding showed strong agreement (κ = 0.82), supporting the feasibility of AI-assisted analysis of perceived psychiatric precipitants.

articles_hidden.title: Post-Encoding Semantic Processing Produces Systematic Distortions in Episodic Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Katelyn G. Cliver; Kennedy N King; Alexa Tompary
articles_hidden.abstract: How new experiences can update a memory has important consequences for its long-term storage, but little is known about how different kinds of re exposure may differentially influence its content. Inspired by theories of memory reconstruction that posit that memory retrieval depends on the integration of idiosyncratic details and relevant general knowledge, we investigated how exposure to a memory through category- or item-level processing may strengthen its episodic and semantic components. Across three behavioral experiments, participants encoded image-location associations in a protocol designed to generate a conflict between memory for specific images and knowledge of the general location of other images from the same category. Following learning of the locations, participants completed manipulations aimed to prioritize category-level or item-level processing of the images. We hypothesized that requiring semantic processing after learning would reinforce prior category knowledge associated with each image and increase category-driven distortions in memory at test. Our findings revealed that memory for images that underwent semantic processing were less precise and more distorted relative to memories that underwent item-level processing and relative to those that were not re-exposed after encoding. Furthermore, post-encoding manipulations more strongly updated memories of atypical category members, suggesting that the organization of prior knowledge can govern the extent that new memories can be updated. Together, these results highlight the active role of post‑encoding manipulations in differentially reshaping memory content and provide compelling evidence that episodic memory retrieval is a constructive process that integrates across prior knowledge, discrete experiences, and subsequent re-exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Are males victims of intimate partner violence in Greece? Prevalence of the phenomenon and implications for mental health
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiota Peleka; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Ioannis Moisoglou; Angeliki Triantafillaki; Olympia Konstantakopoulou; Anastasia Tsalouka; Maria Tsiachri; Antigoni Kolisiati; Petros Galanis
articles_hidden.abstract: OBJECTIVE To investigate the association between intimate partner violence (IPV) and mental health among males in a Greek population. METHODS A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Greece in July 2026. IPV among males was assessed using the Woman Abuse Screening Tool (WAST), while the lifetime prevalence of physical, psychological/emotional, and sexual abuse was evaluated through three dichotomous self-report items (yes/no). Anxiety-like and depressive-like symptoms were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4). Sleep quality was assessed with the Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS), self-esteem with the Single-Item Self-Esteem Scale (SISE), loneliness with the UCLA 3-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-LS-3), and life satisfaction with the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS).
