To account for the potential influence of demographic characteristics, multivariable linear regression analyses were performed with adjustment for relevant demographic confounding variables. RESULTS In the adjusted model, higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms. Additionally, levels of anxiety-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Multivariable model found that higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of depressive-like symptoms. Additionally, levels of depressive-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Sleep quality was worse among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of self-esteem. Additionally, levels of self-esteem were lower among males that have experienced physical abuse through their lives. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of loneliness. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of life satisfaction. Additionally, levels of life satisfaction were lower among males that have experienced psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. CONCLUSIONS IPV was significantly associated with poorer mental health and psychosocial well-being among males in Greece. Greater exposure to abusive behaviors was associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms, depressive-like symptoms, and loneliness, as well as poorer sleep quality, lower self-esteem, and reduced life satisfaction. These findings highlight the substantial psychological burden associated with IPV and underscore its detrimental impact on multiple dimensions of mental health and well-being among male victims.

articles_hidden.title: Simulation-based cutoffs for conditional item fit in Rasch models: iterations, multiplicity correction, and decision stability
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Simulation-based cutoff values for conditional item fit can be estimated by parametric bootstrapping
and reported as an interval of a chosen width. Johansson (2025) recommended this
over rule-of-thumb critical values and gave iteration guidance based on detection rates and
conditioned on sample size, without an account of the error rate that the interval width controls.
This paper re-examines iterations and width against the familywise error rate (FWER),
and compares FWER and false discovery rate control. Seven simulation studies vary item count
and the targeting of misfitting items, with both dichotomous and polytomous conditions.

The interval width is shown to be the error rate parameter of the procedure, setting the
FWER jointly with the number of items. Bootstrap p-values with a Westfall-Young FWER
correction target that error rate directly, detect more misfit than a width-matched interval,
and are calibrated from 400 iterations, with fewer false positives than Benjamini-Hochberg.
Outfit was consistently less powerful than infit, confirming earlier dichotomous findings and
extending them to polytomous items.

Updated recommendations include flagging items on the Westfall-Young FWER corrected
p-value, using at least 400 iterations and 1000 to 2000 for a final analysis, and reporting the
interval as a descriptive band at width .95. The described methods are available in the R
package easyRasch2 and the jamovi module easyRasch2jmv.

articles_hidden.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Valentin Emslander; Oliver Adam Kluge; Christoph Niepel
articles_hidden.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

articles_hidden.title: The FlexER-Scale: A new Self-report Measure of Individual Differences in Emotion Regulation Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel; Timo Schweikert; Denise Dörfel
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research on emotion regulation (ER) has primarily focused on individual strategies and their association with well-being and psychopathology. Recent frameworks emphasize a context-sensitive, goal-dependent approach, defining ER flexibility as the ability to adaptively adjust ER strategies based on contextual demands and personal goals. Despite growing evidence for its relevance, a concise self-report measure designed to capture trait-level, strategy-independent ER flexibility has been lacking. To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) and validated it using data from four independent samples (N = 1,019). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample examined the scale’s structure; criterion validity was assessed via correlations with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). The final 10-item FlexER-Scale demonstrated good psychometric properties, including satisfactory item discrimination and high internal consistency (α = .85). EFA suggested a two-factor structure differentiating hedonic and contra-hedonic ER flexibility, which was supported by CFA. The FlexER-Scale showed a significant positive correlation with psychological well-being, driven by the hedonic factor. Small but significant correlations with habitual reappraisal and suppression use provided initial evidence for discriminant validity. The FlexER-Scale is a promising tool for assessing ER flexibility, offering a concise alternative to existing measures by capturing adaptive regulatory variability without relying on predefined strategies. Future research should examine its construct validity, longitudinal stability, and predictive validity. Given that the validation was based on predominantly student samples from a German-speaking context, broader generalizability remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Using a Foreign Language Does Not Make the Art More Profound - Familiarity Does
articles_hidden.authors: Wojciech Milczarski; Anna Borkowska; Susanne Brouwer; Michal Bialek
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated whether using a foreign language affects aesthetic judgments of art. Across three experiments (N=345), Polish-English and Dutch-English bilinguals rated songs and paintings on profoundness, liking, recommendation, and familiarity. Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings). Contrary to theoretical predictions based on reduced emotional engagement and impaired metacognition in foreign languages, presentation language did not significantly affect any ratings. Instead, two factors consistently predicted profoundness judgments: familiarity and medium. Participants rated familiar artworks as more profound regardless of language condition, and music received higher profoundness ratings than paintings across all experiments. These findings suggest that aesthetic perception is primarily driven by prior exposure and medium-specific characteristics rather than the language in which art is encountered, challenging assumptions about linguistic effects on aesthetic judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Power-law Behaviour in Eye Movements During Reading in 21 Languages
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Fabian
articles_hidden.abstract: Eye movements provide insights into psychological processes. In reading research, investigating cognitive processes via differences in reading behaviour is prevalent. However, cross-linguistic universalities in eye movement behaviour during reading remain largely unknown. A recent study analysed relations between successive eye movements, designated relative saccade lengths, and found that the relations' probability distributions observe a power-law-shaped tail across various tasks and experiments, including reading in six different languages. Validating this finding and assessing its universality for further languages is essential since it could represent the first language-independent and quantifiable statistical regularity in reading behaviour. With existing data from the MECO corpus, we replicate the original study's results with further empirical data for the same six languages and extend the analyses to a total of 21 languages (N = 1299). The results show that the probability distributions of relative saccade lengths consistently observe a power-law-shaped tail across all 21 languages. Thus, our results replicate the findings of the original study's six languages and extend them to 15 further languages. This provides further empirical evidence for the probability distribution of relative saccade lengths as a possible universality in eye movement behaviour during reading. Furthermore, the slope of the probability distributions suggests that adjusting eye movement lengths during reading might constitute optimal search behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Workplace Greenery and Work Engagement Among Live-In Shiftworkers: A Conceptual Replication of Popov et al. (2023)
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Isabelle Ekeberg; Kristin Kloster; Peder Mortvedt Isager
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents a conceptual replication of @popov2023 (Study 2), examining whether workplace greenery is associated with work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context. Ninety-four live-in shiftworkers (55.3% women) employed in Norwegian assisted living facilities for adults with intellectual disabilities and/or autism spectrum disorders completed an online survey during autumn 2024. Work engagement was measured with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale, and three forms of workplace greenery were assessed: window views of nature, access to outdoor natural environments, and the presence of indoor plants. Analyses of covariance, controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty, largely replicated the original pattern of results. Access to outdoor natural environments—both during breaks and while accompanying service users—was significantly associated with higher work engagement, whereas window views and indoor plants showed no reliable effects. Gender did not consistently moderate these associations. The findings provide evidence that the association between outdoor nature exposure and work engagement may extend to live-in shiftworkers and an autumn context.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People-Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing (i.e., the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others) has recently attracted considerable attention in popular psychology. Empirical research has been devoted only recently to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous Graded Response Model (N = 2,538). The three-factor solution (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) elicited sufficient model and item fit and predominant support for the assumption of local independence. Its three subscales provided favorable item discrimination and threshold parameters indicating that endorsement of the highest response categories requires only moderately elevated levels of people-pleasing. Seven of the 10 items provided information across comparatively broad regions of the latent trait continuum, albeit with lower peak information. These findings illustrate candidate items for future scale shortening without substantial loss of measurement precision.

articles_hidden.title: Working Memory Development: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Analyses of Primary School Children in an Adaptive Learning Environment
articles_hidden.authors: Şeyma Nur Ertekin; Abe Dirk Hofman; Evie Vergauwe; Julia M. Haaf
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study investigated the spatial working memory (WM) ability and its developmental change, utilizing large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data from an adaptive learning environment. Approximately 16% of Dutch primary school children participated in a spatial serial recall task between 2019 and 2025, providing dense, continuous measurements of the same children in their regular educational environment. Cross-sectional analyses demonstrated the increase of working memory capacity between the ages of six and twelve on average by one item. However, the spatial complexity of the lists affected this capacity increase. Moreover, longitudinal analyses of accuracy demonstrated WM ability maturation over time, yet there was no impact of practicing the task. Furthermore, significant individual differences were observed among children. Future studies should focus on a better assessment of spatial complexity and the underlying sources for individual differences in WM development.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Abilities and Trust Calibration: Understanding Individual Differences in Automation Trust Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Connie Ku; Anne Collins McLaughlin; Richard Pak; Randall W Engle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people develop and maintain trust
in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly
understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities — working
memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) — shape trust dynamics,
particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (n=111)
completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm
where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-
65%-100%) while completing a mental arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf
positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust
calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system
reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting immediacy of trust
loss. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by
automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about
automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust
dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema
updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This
work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing
automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

articles_hidden.title: Further Psychometric Evaluation of the Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) Scale and Validation of a German Version.
articles_hidden.authors: David Scholz; Johannes Kraus
articles_hidden.abstract: The Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) scale by Scholz et al. (2025) provides a psychometrically sound instrument for assessing individual differences in the propensity to trust in automated systems. To date, however, the scale has only been validated in its original English version. The present study aimed to validate both the 14-item and 6-item versions of the scale in German. Furthermore, given the lack of validated measures of PTT-A with established measurement invariance (MI) across languages and gender, we examined whether the scale permits meaningful comparisons across these groups, thereby facilitating cross-cultural research on trust in automation. To this end, the PTT-A scale was translated into German, and its psychometric properties were evaluated in a large-scale online study (N = 1,629). In addition to examining the German versions, we assessed the psychometric properties of the original English versions and tested MI across language (English vs. German) and gender (female vs. male) using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis. The results supported the psychometric properties of both the 14-item and 6-item versions in English and German. Furthermore, sufficient MI was established across language and gender, supporting the comparability of scale scores between the respective groups. Overall, the findings provide a validated German version of the PTT-A scale in both its full and short forms. The evidence for MI across language and gender further supports its use in cross-language research and comparisons of propensity to trust in automation across these groups.

articles_hidden.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: Valerio Capraro; Gary Marcus; Walter Quattrociocchi
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

articles_hidden.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles_hidden.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing measurement in adaptive learning systems: How much can we gain from response times?
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Bolsinova; Jesper Tijmstra; Matthieu J. S. Brinkhuis; Abe Dirk Hofman; Bence Gergely
articles_hidden.abstract:
Obtaining accurate measures of changing abilities is essential for online adaptive learning systems (ALS) to provide learners with instructional material and practice items at the appropriate level. 
Despite the large data volume in ALS, focusing on a single individual at a specific moment yields limited data, reducing measurement precision. To improve quality of measurement in ALS, it has been proposed to incorporate response time (RT) data into measurement (Klinkenberg et al., 2011). Using data from an ALS for primary school mathematics Math Garden (Straatemeier, 2014), we compare different models that incorporate RTs and can be used for ability tracking with each other and with the benchmark Rasch model, in which ability is measured based only on the accuracy of the responses. We also contrast these empirical findings with simulation results that match the empirical setup but where the generating model matches the way in which RTs are incorporated into measurement, to study what can be gained under ideal circumstances. Our results show that while theoretical gains are large, in the studied empirical setting RTs at best provide a modest improvement that was not fully consistent across domains and depended on the reward system implemented in the ALS. Implications of the results for the choice of the measurement model in ALS are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Covert consciousness is not cognitive motor dissociation and the vegetative state is not a state of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Martin M Monti; Caroline Schnakers; Nicholas D. Schiff; Yelena G Bodien
articles_hidden.abstract: The discovery of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) has revealed a conceptual inconsistency at the heart of disorders of consciousness (DoC) nosology. Advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that behavioral unresponsiveness does not necessarily imply the absence of consciousness or cognitive capacity, yet contemporary diagnostic categories continue equating unresponsiveness with unconsciousness. This equivalence is embedded throughout DoC nomenclature, where behavioral syndromes such as the vegetative state (VS) and minimally conscious state (MCS) are defined by what patients are inferred to experience (i.e., their state of mind) but operationalized on the basis of what they are observed to do (or not do). We argue that this category error now impedes the translation of over two decades of scientific advances into a coherent clinical framework. First, it has fostered the widespread but incorrect conflation of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), despite the fact that the two concepts identify different patient populations and may carry distinct implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Second, it renders contemporary DoC nosology incapable of coherently incorporating modern neuroimaging and electrophysiological findings. Because the absence of consciousness is an entrenched, definitional component of the VS, its behavioral phenotype cannot be reconciled with covert neurophysiological phenotypes such as CC and CMD. As a result, current nomenclature impedes the development of a phenotype-endotype framework in which bedside behavioral classifications are complemented by biologically informed categories derived from advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological assessments. We trace the origins of this problem to a historical shift whereby the definitions of VS and MCS evolved from descriptions of observable behavior into claims about a patient’s mental state. Disentangling responsiveness from consciousness, we argue, is essential if the field is to incorporate contemporary evidence and develop a coherent, biologically informed nosology of DoC, which, in our view, is best pursued within a phenotype-endotype framework.

articles_hidden.title: The Formation of the Sufferer: Deconstructive Inquiry and the Self-Problem Relation in Psychotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Arie Todd Greenleaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy generally begins with a person who has a problem and needs help resolving it. Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) examines how the struggle to resolve a difficulty can form the apparent self who must overcome it. This conceptual paper draws on a relational ontology, which understands things as organized patterns of relations. The self who must overcome fear, for example, takes shape through judging, resisting, and trying to escape fear. This activity is experienced as someone separate from the feeling and responsible for ending it. I call this formation centering. Comparison with a remembered past or imagined future can sustain the struggle by making present life unacceptable until the person changes. DI proposes that the effort and its apparent controller can become recognizable as the same activity. The division need not continue, even while fear remains and the person responds to what needs attention. A composite clinical vignette illustrates this possibility and shows how the therapist’s need to prove helpful can reinforce the client’s struggle. I also propose that insight changes the knowledge shaping later encounters, allowing change to persist without requiring the person to recall or repeat the insight. Comparisons with other therapies examine whether a separate observing self remains when therapy succeeds. The paper considers how cultural expectations shape these struggles and how therapists and supervisors can participate in sustaining or questioning them.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Menstrual Cycle Phase in PTSD: A Scoping Review of Symptom Expression, Neuropsychology and Psychotherapy Response in Women
articles_hidden.authors: Ciara Treacy; Mia Schaumberg; Katherine Moore; Ella Liow; Sophie Andrews; Bronwyn Graham; Alain Brunet
articles_hidden.abstract: Women are diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) at twice the rate of men, a disparity only partly explained by trauma exposure differences. Sex-specific biological factors, particularly cyclic fluctuations in estradiol and progesterone, have been associated with PTSD symptoms/related neuropsychological processes in healthy/trauma exposed women; however, the extent and clinical translation of this literature (if any) remain unclear in PTSD populations. This review aimed to map evidence examining associations between ovarian hormones/menstrual cycle phase and PTSD symptoms and/or related neuropsychological processes (e.g., extinction learning) in women with PTSD (Aim1), and/or associations with psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD/related anxiety disorders (Aim2). A systematic search for peer-reviewed, empirical studies involving adult females was conducted across 6 databases, in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines. From 2,464 results, 12 studies were included. Five studies addressed Aim 1 and seven addressed Aim 2. Hormonal operationalization was inconsistent, including continuous assays (n=5), menstrual cycle phase comparisons (n=3), and/or median split/other groupings (n=6), with estradiol most frequently measured. For Aim 1, PTSD symptom findings were inconsistent and inconclusive (n=3), whereas lower estradiol was more consistently associated with impaired fear extinction and habituation (n=2). For Aim 2, findings in anxiety-related disorders were mixed, with no study examining ovarian hormone status in psychotherapy outcomes for women with PTSD. Overall, evidence remains sparse, heterogeneous and largely cross-sectional. Findings do not yet support firm conclusions regarding ovarian hormone–PTSD symptom/neuropsychological interactions but highlight key research gaps and future directions to better understand these relationships and inform personalized PTSD treatments for women.

articles_hidden.title: Video games in cognitive event-related EEG research: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Belinda Fleischmann; Sean Mulready; Dirk Ostwald
articles_hidden.abstract: Event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on controlled laboratory tasks with limited ecological validity. Video games offer a middle ground between laboratory and real-world settings, combining intuitive interaction with experimental control. This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, characterizes video game paradigms used in event-related EEG research and relates their findings to canonical laboratory effects. Database and supplementary searches identified 29 studies using 26 paradigms. Most paradigms used custom-built games and required visuomotor navigation or targeting within continuous gameplay, and most analyses were time-locked to feedback events such as hits or collisions. Findings showed selective convergence with laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, and for movement-related activity. Evidence for error- and feedback-related components was more limited, while early sensory responses were rarely examined. We discuss emerging patterns in the use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms, the correspondence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, and the methodological challenges of studying event-related activity during gameplay. In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about neural responses during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.

articles_hidden.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Schafer; Emmett M. Larsen; Kiyohito Iigaya; Guillermo Horga
articles_hidden.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond individual features: Identifying computational principles in perceiving visual beauty
articles_hidden.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci; Philipp Flieger; Daniel Kaiser
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape. Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains. Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty. Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain. We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles. First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding. Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings. Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data. We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches. In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the psychometric properties of depression and social-emotional functioning measures with autistic adolescents and their parents
articles_hidden.authors: My H Vu; Elika Parab; Vana Matevosian; Pia Hernandez; Jessica Schwartzman
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. facing greater risks for depression and adverse mental health outcomes than the general population of youth. The psychometric properties of most measures remain untested with autistic youth even though autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity including unique cognitive, affective, behavioral and sensory needs. The present study tested the internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, convergent and discriminant validity, and cross-informant agreement between 101 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) and their parents for several depression and social-emotional functioning measures (e.g., social motivation, anhedonia/apathy). Most measures showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across informants, while confirmatory factor analyses yielded mixed evidence of structural validity. Convergent validity was moderate and adolescent and parent reports agreed poorly to moderately, which emphasizes the value of collecting both perspectives. Findings inform clinical practice by supporting the continued use of several measures in autistic adolescents, while suggesting caution in interpreting others.

articles_hidden.title: Rest-Activity Rhythms, Social Interaction, and Depressive Symptoms in Older Adults: A Longitudinal Within- and Between-Person Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction have each been linked to late-life depression, yet their independent longitudinal contributions have rarely been examined within a framework separating between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. This study examined their independent associations with depressive symptoms in community-dwelling older adults.
Method: Data from Rounds 12–14 (2022–2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) included 1,532 person-wave observations from 606 participants. A Behavioral Rhythm Index (BRI) combined mean activity, relative amplitude, and reversed day-to-day variability. Person-mean-centered random-intercept linear mixed models separated within- from between-person associations, adjusting for wave, age, sex, and education.
Results: Higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.238, p < .001) and within persons (B = −0.139, p = .013), although the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses. Greater social interaction was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.714, p < .001) but not within persons. BRI and social interaction did not significantly interact (χ²(2) = 2.05, p = .359).
Conclusion: Higher BRI and greater habitual social engagement were each independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals, warranting further investigation as potentially modifiable behavioral factors in late-life depression.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: The Emotion Filmmaker: Temporal Memory, Time-Emotion Integration, and Affective Style
articles_hidden.authors: Mengsi Li; Regina C Lapate
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional experiences are temporally dynamic, but prior work suggests that temporal features are usually neglected in remembered emotion. For instance, retrospective emotion evaluations are often biased by discrete salient timepoints, such as the peak and end moments, at the expense of objective event duration (i.e., peak–end effects and duration neglect). However, how these retrospective emotion biases originate, as well as their significance for emotional functioning, remain unclear. Here, we test the hypothesis that retrospective emotion biases are related to fundamental limits of temporal processing and memory capacity. Further, we examine whether these limits have implications for emotional functioning. Participants (n = 60) underwent a novel paradigm comprising affectively-rich movie sequences while providing emotion ratings continuously (moment-by-moment) and retrospectively. Temporal memory for previously-watched emotional-movie sequences and dispositional negativity were measured. Our findings revealed a greater “end” bias as the duration of emotional-movie sequences increased, suggesting that limitations in temporal processing capacity may contribute to retrospective emotion biases. Critically, temporal-memory errors were associated with larger retrospective emotion biases and with individual differences in dispositional negativity. Collectively, these results indicate that retrospective emotion biases may stem partly from mnemonic temporal errors that are emotionally maladaptive.

articles_hidden.title: Barriers to professional mental health help-seeking and considerations for school-based interventions among Secondary School adolescents: an exploratory qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Christianah Dada
articles_hidden.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Professional mental health service use remains low among adolescents, and school-based interventions are frequently designed without consulting the young people and clinicians they are intended to serve. This exploratory qualitative study investigated the specific barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents to inform the development of a culturally relevant school-based intervention. Following the ethical principles of the Belmont Report, a focus group discussion was conducted with ten secondary school students (aged 13–16), alongside individual in-depth interviews with two students and key informant interviews with two practicing clinical psychologists in Ibadan, Nigeria. Audio-recorded transcripts were verified and examined utilizing thematic analysis. Eight core categories emerged from the data, highlighting a limited formal understanding of mental health among youth and a prominent gap between baseline knowledge and help-seeking behaviors. While distress including depression, anxiety, addiction, and trauma was widely recognized through behavioral or academic declines, pervasive stigma and the fear of diagnostic labeling acted as dominant barriers to care, with nine out of ten adolescents refusing professional care pathways. Friends served as primary confidants, while parental spiritual beliefs heavily gatekept formal psychological interventions. Social media heavily informed adolescent self-image but introduced acute body-image concerns. Notably, one student preferred using an artificial intelligence chatbot over human contact to ensure absolute confidentiality. Participants requested foundational mental health literacy and coping skills delivered via brief, visual, interactive sessions, while clinicians anticipated systemic institutional implementation challenges regarding school leadership, funding deficits, and staffing constraints. Interventions must target social stigma and privacy constraints directly alongside conceptual awareness.

articles_hidden.title: Does autonomy enhance satisfaction, adherence and clinical outcomes? A Randomized Controlled Trial of a digital mental health intervention for college students
articles_hidden.authors: Sevin Ozmen; Leonore de Wit; Arpana Amarnath; Annemieke van Straten; Sascha Y Struijs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: College students face high rates of mental health problems including depression and stress. Digital interventions offer accessible support, but adherence remains challenging. Autonomy may enhance motivation, yet its role in student-focused digital interventions is not explored yet in a randomized controlled trial. 
Objective: This study examines whether enhancing autonomy in a guided digital CBT-based mental health intervention for college students (LifeHack) improves satisfaction, adherence, and mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a two-armed randomized trial, 575 students were assigned to either a structured intervention or an autonomy-enhanced version in which participants could select topics of interest. Assessments were conducted at baseline and 5 weeks later (post-intervention). Primary outcomes were general satisfaction (CSQ-8) and working alliance with the program and e-coach (WAI-I); secondary outcomes included adherence, mental well-being (MHC-SF), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and quality of life (MHQoL). 
Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen’s d ranging 0.24-0.41). However, no significant differences were observed between conditions on satisfaction, adherence or clinical outcomes.
Conclusions: Allowing users to freely choose lesson topics did not enhance satisfaction, adherence, or clinical outcomes compared with a structured lesson sequence. Nonetheless, participation in LifeHack was associated with improved mental health, indicating potential intervention effectiveness regardless of the autonomy features. Future research should test more comprehensive autonomy-supportive designs and compare LifeHack with inactive control conditions to establish intervention effectiveness.

articles_hidden.title: Interindividual Differences in Treatment Effects of a Personality Change Intervention on Life and Domain Satisfaction
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Kroencke; Johannes Zimmermann; Saskia Baumgardt; Lena Brüggmann; Claudia Harzer; Axel Mayer; Mirjam Stieger; Lara Puhlmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality change interventions have shown promising average effects not only on personality traits, but also on well-being. However, little is known about the extent to which these effects differ between individuals and what baseline characteristics are associated with such differences. To answer these questions, we analyzed data from the PEACH intervention, a 10-week smartphone-based personality change intervention (N = 873). Using the EffectLiteR framework for causal inference, we estimated average and individual treatment effects of the intervention (vs. waitlist) on life satisfaction, average life domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains. Moreover, we tested whether interindividual differences in treatment effects could be predicted by demographic characteristics, baseline personality traits, baseline well-being, motivational factors, and engagement preferences. We found a significant average treatment effect on average domain satisfaction (d = 0.20), concentrated in work- and emotion-related domains, but not life satisfaction. Notably, we identified significant heterogeneity in this effect across participants: For approximately 27% of participants, the PEACH intervention showed positive effects on average domain satisfaction, while for 66% it showed no effects, and for 7% it showed negative effects. Men, individuals rated higher in Openness by observers, and individuals with lower self-reported change goal attainability at baseline benefited most from the intervention. Taken together, these findings suggest that personality change interventions can enhance domain satisfaction for some, but not all, individuals, underscoring the need for personalized approaches and the identification of subgroups for whom interventions may be ineffective or even counterproductive.

articles_hidden.title: The Formation of the Sufferer: Deconstructive Inquiry and the Self-Problem Relation in Psychotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Arie Todd Greenleaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy generally begins with a person who has a problem and needs help resolving it. Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) examines how the struggle to resolve a difficulty can form the apparent self who must overcome it. This conceptual paper draws on a relational ontology, which understands things as organized patterns of relations. The self who must overcome fear, for example, takes shape through judging, resisting, and trying to escape fear. This activity is experienced as someone separate from the feeling and responsible for ending it. I call this formation centering. Comparison with a remembered past or imagined future can sustain the struggle by making present life unacceptable until the person changes. DI proposes that the effort and its apparent controller can become recognizable as the same activity. The division need not continue, even while fear remains and the person responds to what needs attention. A composite clinical vignette illustrates this possibility and shows how the therapist’s need to prove helpful can reinforce the client’s struggle. I also propose that insight changes the knowledge shaping later encounters, allowing change to persist without requiring the person to recall or repeat the insight. Comparisons with other therapies examine whether a separate observing self remains when therapy succeeds. The paper considers how cultural expectations shape these struggles and how therapists and supervisors can participate in sustaining or questioning them.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing conditionals: An experimental comparison of suppositional and inferential accounts
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandro Bogani; Andrea Iacona; Stefania Pighin; Vincenzo Crupi; Katya Tentori
articles_hidden.abstract: Two main normative accounts have been proposed to explain the acceptability of a conditional. The suppositional account equates acceptability with the probability of the consequent given the antecedent, whereas the inferential account maintains that it depends on the support the antecedent provides to the consequent. Previous empirical work has addressed the descriptive accuracy of normative and non-normative accounts, but the results have been inconclusive. In the present study, we introduce a novel experimental procedure designed to dissociate the predictions of competing accounts and employ it in three experiments. Overall, the results indicate that most individuals endorse a normative interpretation of conditionals; however, the specific account that best captures their judgments depends on the type of conditional evaluated. For conditionals in which the antecedent and the consequent stand in an arbitrary relation (e.g., “If the toy is a triangle, then it will be yellow”), judgments align more closely with the suppositional account. In contrast, for conditionals where the antecedent and the consequent are directly causally related (e.g., “If the laser is misaligned, then the prosthesis will have cracks” or “If the prosthesis has cracks, then the laser was misaligned”), judgments are better captured by the inferential account. Possible extensions of current models aimed at achieving a comprehensive characterization of conditionals are briefly discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The Strengths and Pitfalls of No-report Paradigms in Multistable Perception Research
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel van der Meer; Simon van Gaal; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas; Michael D. Nunez
articles_hidden.abstract: Ambiguous, multistable stimuli can give rise to multiple perceptual interpretations. Bistable visual stimuli, in particular, have long been used to study neurological and cognitive processes. However, many experimental paradigms rely on self-report to assess subjective perceptual experiences, introducing potential issues such as low reliability and interferences of reporting into the processes under investigation. No-report paradigms serve as a method to work around these problems by decoding perceptual content based on physiological data. Here we discuss the strengths and pitfalls of no-report paradigms in the context of research using multistable perception. Focusing on experimental power related to decoding accuracy, we exemplify the current progress of decoding perceptual content using three major domains of physiological data (eye-tracking, M/EEG and fMRI). We find that the predictability of the percept varies significantly depending on the paradigm and stimulus type, showcasing both the potential and limitations of physiological inference in bistable perception research.

articles_hidden.title: Sensory Processing in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Luszawski; Caroline Luszawski; Natalie Luszawski; Blake Edward Butler; Bobby Stojanoski; Jason Brown; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a range of developmental differences following the exposure of alcohol in utero. Although not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion for FASD, sensory processing deficits are commonly observed in individuals with FASD. The purpose of this scoping review was to review the existing evidence regarding the sensory processing differences in individuals with FASD compared to neurotypical individuals. A scoping review of the literature was conducted investigating studies of human participants with FASD and neurotypical participants. Studies were included if they reported on sensory processing differences between FASD and neurotypical participants. Any measures of sensory processing and in-utero exposure to alcohol were included. APA Psycinfo, Embase, Medline, Scopus, and CINAHL were searched for relevant studies. A total of 1192 studies were screened for inclusion, of which 42 were extracted. Studies investigated sensory processing differences in unisensory visual, auditory, olfactory, and somatosensory processing, multisensory integration, and sensorimotor processing. Measures of sensory processing included imaging measures (fMRI, MRI), clinical interviews, questionnaires, behavioural tasks, psychometric tests, and electrophysiological measures (EEG, MEG, DTI). Results indicate that differences in sensory processing exist in individuals with FASD when compared to neurotypical controls; however, these differences may vary depending on the age of participants, the type of sensory processing being measured, and other individual participant factors.

articles_hidden.title: Eye See Your Intentions: Age-Related Differences in Gaze Perception and Trustworthiness Attributions
articles_hidden.authors: Alayna Shoenfelt; Reese E. Chadwick; Tian Lin; Sanghee Park; Teodoro Ayub Barres; Natalie C. Ebner
articles_hidden.abstract: Successful social interactions depend on regulating approach-avoidance tendencies as well as accurately understanding those motivations in others. Direct gaze signals approach intentions, whereas averted gaze signals avoidance intentions. Older relative to younger adults display a stronger direct gaze bias (i.e., are more likely to perceive eye gaze as direct vs. averted). This bias in motivational cue perception likely impacts social trait attributions. This study, for the first time, leveraged a lifespan sample across a wide age range (18 – 88 years; N = 307) to investigate adult lifespan differences in gaze perception using a novel set of gaze-modified face stimuli with varying expressions and tested whether perception of gaze aversion affected attributions of facial trustworthiness. Participants were recruited and the study conducted online via Prolific. Faces with more averted gaze were perceived as more direct-looking with age. This bias was relatively weaker for fearful faces compared to all other facial expressions. Further, greater perception of direct gaze was associated with greater facial trustworthiness attributions, and especially with age. Combined, these findings confirm a direct gaze bias in aging and support its impact on social trait attributions. These adult lifespan differences in approach-avoidance motivational cue perception may reflect shifts in sensitivity, capacity, and/or motivation and are discussed as a possible mechanism in greater trust and susceptibility to deception with age. This work also adds substantially to the widely used FACES Lifespan Database corpus by making the newly gaze-modified faces, and their norm ratings, publicly available for research on motivational and cognitive aging.

articles_hidden.title: Methodological Flexibility in the Iowa Gambling Task Undermines Interpretability: A Meta-method Review
articles_hidden.authors: Annika Iris Külpmann; Jan-Paul Ries; Ian Hussey; Malte Elson
articles_hidden.abstract: Methodological flexibility–researcher degrees of freedom in procedure and scoring–can contribute to poor measurement and low replicability of findings. To quantify methodological flexibility in the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT), a widely used measure of decision-making in clinical psychology, we conducted a meta-method review of a random sample of 100 studies. We found prevalent under-reporting and wide-spread modifications of procedural details. We identified 244 distinct scores used to quantify IGT outcomes, 177 of which appeared only once in our sample. To quantify the potential impact of this flexibility, we performed a multiverse analysis using 205 scores on an open IGT dataset. Correlations among these ranged from rs = -0.942 to 0.998 with a median r = 0.022, suggesting that different scoring strategies can produce extremely different study outcomes. Given these findings, without substantive information about which specific procedural and scoring choices were employed, results from the IGT are rendered uninterpretable. Supplementary Materials, Data, and Code are available at github.com/anniria/igt-methodological-flexibility.

articles_hidden.title: Growing Well with Grow It!: Acceptability of a Gamified mHealth App for Adolescents With a Chronic Somatic Illness – A Mixed Methods Study
articles_hidden.authors: Marije van Dalen; Hanneke Scholten; Inge Braspenning; Loes Keijsers; Johanna Wilhelmina Weerdmeester; Jeroen Legerstee; Manon H.J. Hillegers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Over 17% of children live with a chronic somatic illness and are at increased risk of experiencing psychological problems, such as anxiety and depression. Grow It! is a transdiagnostic mobile health (mHealth) intervention that combines experience sampling and personalised mood feedback with daily coping challenges to promote reflection, emotional insight and adaptive coping. The app fosters a collaborative team experience in which participants contribute to growing a shared virtual tree and communicate through a chat function with predesigned stickers. 
Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the acceptability of the Grow It! app among adolescents with a chronic somatic illness and to identify key lessons the development of other gamified mHealth apps designed to promote well-being.
Methods: This preregistered study is part of a randomised waitlist controlled trial. Adolescents with a chronic somatic illness aged 10-18 years old were recruited from a university medical children’s hospital. Upon inclusion, adolescents were randomised to an intervention group that used the Grow It! app or a waitlist control group. Follow up questionnaires were completed immediately after the four week intervention period and three months later. Consecutively, the waitlist control group was also offered the Grow It! app and completed questionnaires immediately after use and three months later. Participants completed user experience survey comprising open ended and closed questions after playing the app. Responses were analysed using qualitative content analysis and descriptive statistics.
Results: Between August 2021 and September 2023, 208 adolescents were included in the study. Due to participant attrition, the user experience survey was distributed to 183 participants and completed by 150 (Mage=13.95, 39.33% male, 59.33% female, 1.33% other). The app received a mean overall rating of 7.32 out of 10, and a mean look-and-feel rating of 7.98 out of 10; 84% would recommend the app to a friend. Participants reported that the app helped them recognise their emotions and gain greater self-insight. They also described its design as colourful and visually appealing. Suggested improvements included adjusting the timing and frequency of the momentary assessments, and expanding the chat function to allow free-text messages or a wider selection of stickers. 
Conclusions: The Grow It! app is well-accepted by adolescents aged 10 to 18 with a chronic somatic illness, although optimising the chat function and reducing questionnaire burden may further improve user experience. Combined with evidence of effectiveness, these findings on acceptability and user experience support the implementation of the Grow It! app in paediatric healthcare.

articles_hidden.title: Analyzing Binary Judgments: An Empirical and Simulation-Based Comparison of Aggregated and Trial-Level Approaches for Hypothesis Testing
articles_hidden.authors: Semih Can Aktepe; Daniel W. Heck
articles_hidden.abstract: Binary judgments are widely used in psychological research to investigate cognitive processes and decision making. Statistical approaches for analyzing such data differ in whether responses are aggregated (e.g., analysis of variance, ANOVA) or modeled at the trial level (e.g., generalized linear mixed models, GLMMs), and in whether results are interpreted as choice proportions or in terms of signal detection theory (SDT) parameters for response bias and discrimination ability. We examined how these approaches differ in specification, interpretation, and results. First, we reanalyzed 20 openly available datasets on the illusory truth effect (212,555 observations), comparing by-subjects (F1) and by-items (F2) ANOVAs of choice proportions, their combination via min-F', a two-step SDT approach (ANOVA of individual SDT estimates), and seven GLMMs with random-effects structures of varying complexity. Second, a Monte Carlo simulation assessed Type I error rates, power, and parameter recovery. GLMMs with random slopes for both participants and items controlled Type I error rates best but often resulted in singular fits. GLMMs with random slopes only for participants were favored by AIC and BIC, but inflated Type I error rates for interactions by ignoring item-specific variability in the repetition effect. Random-intercept-only GLMMs, F1 and F2 ANOVA, and two-step SDT were too liberal for some effects, whereas min-F' was overly conservative. Unlike aggregated analyses, GLMMs account for both participant and item variability and estimate SDT parameters with less bias. We therefore recommend GLMMs with theoretically justified random-effects structure, simplified only if necessary and with the resulting risk of Type I errors for confirmatory hypothesis testing.

articles_hidden.title: A Step-by-Step Tutorial on the Stochastic Cusp Model in R
articles_hidden.authors: Renaud Mabire-Yon; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: People facing similar circumstances may function very differently. The stochastic cusp model offers one possible explanation: the same conditions may support two stable levels of functioning. This tutorial shows how to understand, fit, and interpret the model in R, assuming familiarity with regression and basic R. Simple illustrations explain how stable states emerge and how changing conditions can alter them. A synthetic example links personal resources and acute stress to adaptive functioning. Readers learn to specify the model, check the fit, interpret coefficients and uncertainty, and examine its predictions. At average resources, the fitted distribution changes from one peak at low stress to two separated peaks at higher stress. The tutorial also explains which further observations would help distinguish a cusp hypothesis from competing explanations. Publicly available data, code, and archived output allow readers to reproduce the example.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Distinguishing Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, Cognitive load and Acute Stress in Virtual Reality: Two Randomized and Controlled Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Alexis D. Souchet; Mamadou Lamarana Diallo; Mohammad Soleymani; Domitile Lourdeaux
articles_hidden.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used to study Cognitive load and Acute Stress. But VR comes with side effects such as Cybersickness and Visual fatigue. It remains unclear if we can dissociate psychophysiological responses due to confounding effects. Hence, we conducted two experiments to study and distinguish them. Participants fulfilled a Baseline, Stroop task under four different experimental conditions, Relaxation and Endline. We recorded Stroop performances, Eye tracking (ET), Electrocardiography (ECG), Electrodermal activity (EDA), self-reported Cognitive load, Stress, Cybersickness, Visual fatigue, and Disorientation. Pupil diameter, Blink frequency, Fixations, HR, HRV, and Skin Conductance Response derived between the different conditions. Most of the extracted features from ET, ECG, and EDA showed no differences between states. Despite relaxation steps, Saccade ratio, Blink frequency, Blink duration and Pupil size for ET, Heart rate for ECG, Rise time of the mean skin conductance level, the Arc length of the skin conductance level for EDA were still not back equivalent to baseline. Cognitive load differs from Acute stress based on the Heart rate feature from the ECG sensor. Cognitive load provoked more response with EDA features than Visual fatigue / Cybersickness with the ALSC feature. However, most of those differences have small effect sizes. We underline a 60 minutes immersion “limit.” ET was more sensitive to Visual fatigue / Cybersickness compared to Cognitive load and Acute Stress and ECG to Cognitive load compared to Acute Stress. We documented physiological features varying depending on the state and which one allowed their differentiation. However, side effects can confound other state measures; especially the longer participants are immersed. More experimental inputs are necessary to tackle this research question.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition, Face Processing and Crystallized Intelligence in Personality Pathology: A Multimethod Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ludwig Ohse; Emanuel Jauk; Johannes Zimmermann; André Kerber; Leonie Kampe; Jil Mohr; Robert Schierz; Michael Rentrop; Roeland J. Verhallen; Isabel Dziobek
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality disorders (PDs) are commonly associated with impairments in social cognition, particularly emotion recognition. However, evidence also suggests deficits in more basic cognitive functions, including face processing (e.g., detection of non-emotional facial features) and indicators of general intelligence (e.g., crystallized intelligence). We addressed two exploratory research questions: first, how emotion recognition, face processing, and crystallized intelligence relate to personality pathology across categorical and dimensional PD models, and second, whether these associations primarily reflect general or specific personality pathology. We further hypothesized that the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition would be attenuated when controlling for face processing or crystallized intelligence. In a clinical sample (n = 219), cognitive abilities were assessed using performance-based measures, and personality pathology was assessed using interviews and self-reports. Structural equation modeling, including correlated factor and bifactor-(S-1) models, was applied to separate general from specific personality pathology variance. General personality pathology showed strong negative associations with emotion recognition and small-to-moderate negative associations with face processing and crystallized intelligence. Associations with specific personality pathology were substantially attenuated when controlling for general personality pathology. The link between personality functioning and emotion recognition was only minimally accounted for by face processing or crystallized intelligence. These findings suggest that cognitive deficits in PD may primarily reflect severity rather than disorder-specific variance, while the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition appears not to be reducible to face processing or crystallized intelligence. Our study suggests that dimensional models provide a more nuanced framework for understanding cognitive impairment in personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: Catatonia recovery separates two intervention axes that constrain electroconvulsive therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles_hidden.abstract: A treatment can start a recovery or carry one further, and outcomes alone do not say whether these are actions on the same quantity. We ask this of a model motivated by catatonia, in which twenty-five inpatients recovered through five capacities in one fixed order and whose two effective treatments have no known dynamical representation. The model is an evidence-coupled bistable cascade on a dependency chain: each capacity is bistable, the threshold falls as evidence consolidates, and recovery propagates from a root by diffusive coupling. Two quantities are taken as intervention coordinates, an excursion applied to the root and the coupling between adjacent capacities, with the evidence coordinate closed to input by assumption; we show that they act on disjoint regions of state space. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids any non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and in either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so an acute conversion requires an excursion. With the root restored and the downstream chain collapsed, propagation is governed by one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, because the first-stage equilibrium condition factorises; the weakest coupling sets where recovery stops, the same discriminant gives the first-stage eigenvalue and the inverse-square-root passage time through the fold, and the coupling is identifiable from the resting first stage. Eight falsifiable predictions are separated into consequences of the theorems, predictions needing an added clinical correspondence, and predictions needing a latent quantity measured; exploratory comparisons with published data bear on two of them.

articles_hidden.title: Perceiving Interceptive Affordances: How Target Distance, Target Speed and Additional Load Shape Interception Decisions in Football
articles_hidden.authors: John Oyewole; Wiktoria Moskal; Hatty Jones; Harry Ramsey; Helen Nuttall; Christopher Gaffney; Trevor J. Crawford; Sally Linkenauger
articles_hidden.abstract: To perform well, athletes must perceive both individual and social affordances within sporting environments. Interceptive action is often crucial to sporting success, yet research investigating interceptive affordance perception in open-play competitive sporting environments is extremely limited. This novel research investigates how factors such as target distance, target speed, and additional load jointly influence affordance perception for interceptive actions against opponents. Across three pre-registered studies, university level footballers (n = 26) made action-based judgments on whether they could successfully intercept a target moving perpendicularly towards the space between themselves and an opponent. The position of the target systematically varied in its proximity to the participant versus the opponent. Participants consistently displayed proactive interceptive behaviour, persisting with manipulations to target speed, and additional load applied to players and opponents. However, exploratory mixed-effects modelling revealed that participants were sensitive to increases in relative target distance, and additional load, but less sensitive to increases in target speed. These findings have wide ranging implications across many sporting and non-sporting contexts, providing new insights to understanding affordance perception in competitive sporting situations and other fast-paced environments. Additionally, this work has practical applications, highlighting opportunities to explore coaching interventions to enhance interceptive decision-making during matches.

articles_hidden.title: Facial Muscle Responses to Child-Related Emotional Stimuli Among Expecting Fathers, First-Time Fathers, and Fathers With Multiple Children
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja Veistola; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Hannah Spencer; Renate S. M. Buisman; Hanneli Sinisalo; Peter Bos; Mikko J. Peltola
articles_hidden.abstract:
Empathy supports effective caregiving, as parents rely on infants’ non-verbal signals to guide their responses. Emerging evidence suggests that men undergo hormonal and neural changes related to empathy during the transition to parenthood. This study investigated men’s empathic reactions towards children by comparing groups at different stages of fatherhood to test a proposal that expecting and first-time fathers show heightened empathic reactivity to children’s distress. With pre-registered analyses, we compared three groups: expecting fathers (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and fathers of more than one child (N = 39). Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli. Their facial muscle responses were measured using facial electromyography (zygomaticus and corrugator muscles). Participants also reported their subjective emotional reactions and provided saliva samples for testosterone assessment. Only in the Picture task first-time fathers showed stronger corrugator activity to negative child stimuli when compared with expecting fathers, while self-reported empathy did not differentiate the groups. Testosterone was negatively associated with corrugator responses toward negative pictures of children, but only among expecting fathers. Although group differences were modest, these findings point to subtle shifts in fathers’ responsiveness during the transition to parenthood and indicate that early fatherhood may represent a period of heightened responsiveness to child distress.
Keywords: empathy, fatherhood, emotions, electromyography

articles_hidden.title: Is conscious perception necessary to direct attention? A replication of Jiang et al. (2006): Stage 2 Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Yung-Jung Chen; Ryan Bradley Scott; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: The relationship between attention and consciousness has been debated for decades. Observing attentional biases induced by visual stimuli below the conscious threshold is one way of providing evidence for the independence of attention and conscious perception. Among such studies, Jiang et al. (2006) found a strong priming effect below the objective conscious threshold with high sensitivity, in showing attentional biases to nude images suppressed by continuous flash suppression (CFS). In our replication, we found moderate Bayesian evidence for the unconscious attraction from opposite sex nude images below the subjective conscious threshold in heterosexual participants. This supports the theory that attention and consciousness are dissociable, and the idea that sexually attractive visual stimuli capture attention even when rendered unconscious. The results have been checked for computational reproducibility by an independent statistician, full report at https://osf.io/dr35v/files/te58h.

articles_hidden.title: Transparency for Whom? Participants' Informed Consent in the Era of Open Data
articles_hidden.authors: Michela Zambelli; Rossella Caliciuri; Giulia Moncalieri; Angela Sorgente
articles_hidden.abstract: Open data can extend the use of participants’ information far beyond the study for which it was collected, making informed consent for data sharing an important part of research transparency. We examined whether psychology journals that promote open data address this issue in their guidelines and whether articles sharing data report relevant information about consent. We reviewed the websites of 83 journals identified through the TOP Factor list and examined 196 empirical articles sharing data, published in 2024–2025. No journal provided explicit guidance on obtaining consent specifically for sharing participants’ data on open platforms; four required authors to report consent for secondary data use when applicable. Only seven articles (3.57%) provided information connecting informed consent to data sharing, and in six cases this information was identifiable only in repository materials. These findings reveal a transparency gap: consent for data sharing is rarely made explicit in journal guidance or research reports, even when data are openly shared. We recommend clearer communication with participants about data sharing, more detailed reporting and sharing of consent materials, and stronger guidance from journals and institutions.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher Emotions and Instructional Quality—Insights From the Global  Teaching InSights Video Study: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Maximilian Stark; Katrin Lohrmann; Marina Elena Pfeifer; Anne C. Frenzel
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing research into the link between teachers’ emotions and the quality of their lessons has generally relied either on students’ or teachers’ ratings of instructional quality and drawn on teacher samples from homogenous cultural contexts. The present study addressed these limitations by employing data from the multinational Global Teaching InSights study, in which 652 mathematics teachers in eight countries in East Asia, Europe, and South America self-reported their experiences of enjoyment, anger, and anxiety about teaching, and expert raters assessed instructional quality along the three established dimensions of classroom management, socialemotional support, and instructional support. We used fixed-effects linear models to obtain estimates for the covariation between self-reported trait emotions and observer-rated instructional quality dimensions. For social-emotional support, links with teacher anger and teacher anxiety were negative and significant; the link with teacher enjoyment was positive but did not reach statistical significance. These effects were largely homogenous across the international samples, as exploratory analyses revealed. For classroom management and instructional support, effects were negligible in size, and specifically teacher enjoyment–instructional support links were highly internationally heterogeneous. These findings provide essential insights into how teachers’ internal emotional experience translate into their outward instructional behaviors, and the nuances brought about by varying assessment approaches for instructional quality. The observed cross-country variability may spark future cross-national, cross-cultural research in this domain.

articles_hidden.title: A Meta-Analysis of Psychosocial Interventions to Improve Students’ STEM Motivation.
articles_hidden.authors: Jane E Boyle; Geetanjali Basarkod; Johnmarshall Reeve; emily q rosenzweig; Areum Shin; YING MA; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: With global demand for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) skills increasing, education systems seek to increase student motivation in STEM domains. Psychosocial interventions targeting students’ motivational processes represent a promising approach. This meta-analysis synthesized 289 effect sizes across 38 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine the impact of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation. Results indicated a small-to-moderate positive overall effect (g = 0.20). Intervention type did not significantly moderate effects, although effect sizes were higher for personal values (g = 0.33), task value (g = 0.18), and framing interventions (g = 0.18). Motivational construct significantly moderated intervention outcomes with effects observed for competence beliefs (g = 0.36), mindset (g = 0.27), and utility value (g = 0.19), while smaller for interest (g = 0.11), and not significant for cost (g = 0.08, p = 0.088) and goals (g = -0.01, p = 0.85). Gender composition significantly moderated intervention effects with greater benefits observed in samples with higher proportions of female students.
