No significant moderation effects were observed for race, age, educational level, delivery format, country, publication year, peer-review status, or study quality. Qualitative evidence suggested that intervention effects may vary across sociocultural groups, with some indication of stronger responsiveness among first-generation (FG) students and more variable, framing-dependent effects among underrepresented minority (URM) students. These findings imply that psychosocial interventions can enhance STEM motivation when they target competence beliefs, mindset, and utility-value mechanisms, with particularly potential to support groups historically underrepresented in STEM.

articles_hidden.title: Building Research Infrastructure for Meaningful Youth Participation: A Practice-Informed Framework for Participatory Research
articles_hidden.authors: Vera Ellen Heininga; Marloes Dekkers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: While current frameworks present essential principles for effective youth involvement, they provide limited practical advice on how participation can be organized and maintained throughout research projects. Meaningful involvement requires not just chances for youth to engage, but also the structural, relational, and procedural conditions that allow them to have real impact.
Objective: This paper intends to present a practice-based framework for developing research infrastructure that enables meaningful youth involvement and to demonstrate its use across the research process.
Methods: Building upon fifteen years of hands-on experience in youth engagement at Jimmy’s, we adapt a practice-based ecosystem-based model into a framework for participatory research, guided by equity principles and Lundy’s child participation model. The Youth Resilience Groningen study acts as a practical example to demonstrate how this framework can guide the organization of youth engagement, encompassing the formation of partnerships, defined roles, resources, facilitation, co-design, and decision-making processes.
Results: The framework places equity as its main guiding principle and outlines four interrelated pillars: the research organization, researchers and research personnel, emerging research collaborators, and the broader network of community and research allies. These pillars are formed through three parallel processes: Doing, Learning, and Organising. In the Youth Resilience Groningen study, six teens were hired as junior researchers, aided by Jimmy’s, and participated in determining research priorities, creating study materials, developing questionnaires, planning recruitment strategies, and developing educational guest lectures for secondary school classes, delivered as a token of appreciation for their participation in the study. The study demonstrates how organizational structures and continuous support can enable youth participation while addressing ethical, methodological, and institutional limitations.
Conclusion: Effective youth engagement goes beyond just including young individuals in research efforts. It relies on an ecosystem that allows their insights and viewpoints to guide research choices. The practice-based framework provides flexible direction for structuring, overseeing, and enhancing meaningful youth participation in research projects.

articles_hidden.title: How Many Sites, Participants, and Trials? A Tutorial on Multilevel Power Analysis for Multisite Studies with Repeated Measures
articles_hidden.authors: Alicia Franco-Martínez; Miguel A. Vadillo; Ricardo Rey-Sáez
articles_hidden.abstract: Multisite collaborations are increasingly common in psychological science. Planning a multisite study with repeated measures involves more than deciding how many participants to recruit. Researchers must also determine how many sites to include and how many observations to collect from each participant. These decisions become particularly challenging when the experimental effect may vary across both participants and sites. Unfortunately, most widely used power analysis tools do not accommodate the complexity of these structures. In this tutorial, we provide a practical introduction to multilevel power analysis for three-level multisite studies. We first discuss how to identify and model the effect of interest, accounting for different sources of heterogeneity and the population to which researchers intend to generalize their findings. We then demonstrate how to estimate statistical power through simulation using {simr} and how to optimize the number of trials, participants, and sites using {mlpwr}, considering their relative costs. Finally, we illustrate how to explore alternative assumptions about effect size and between-site heterogeneity, verify the power of the selected architecture, assess estimation precision, and calculate the minimum detectable effect size. The accompanying R code provides an adaptable workflow to help researchers plan multisite studies that balance their inferential goals with their available resources.

articles_hidden.title: A FORAY INTO THE UMWELT OF A PREDATORY BACTERIUM
articles_hidden.authors: Pamela Lyon
articles_hidden.abstract:
The concept of Umwelt refers to the phenomenal world of an organism, defined by its senses
and what it does to stay alive, thrive and reproduce. Umwelt had a powerful influence on how
the scientific study of animal behavior under natural conditions developed in the middle
decades of the 20th century and currently is enjoying renewed interest in the field of
comparative cognition. Traditionally, animals have been the exclusive focus of Umwelt-based
analysis. This chapter focuses on Myxococcus xanthus, a predatory bacterium with an unusual,
complex social lifestyle. The presentation is intended to show that the Umwelt concept can be
useful in unpacking, in radically alien forms of life, processes regarded as cognitive in animals
and in a context (predator–prey interactions) long important to ethology and comparative
psychology, where Umwelt has done most work.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the effect of L1, linguistic, and non-linguistic variables on non-word repetition performance of monolingual and multilingual preschool children in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Natalja Ulrich; Julia Jaekel; Nils Jaekel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Increasing linguistic diversity in society means that many children acquire the majority language as an additional language. An important aspect of early language development is phonological processing, yet the factors underlying individual differences in monolingual and multilingual children in these abilities remain poorly understood. 
To investigate these individual differences, the present study examined nonword repetition (NWR) performance in 793 children, including monolingual (n = 637) and multilingual (n = 156, 18 L1s) preschoolers (3-6 years) in Germany. We used mixed-effects models to investigate the role of lexical linguistic distance to German, German exposure, receptive vocabulary, and morphological skills on NWR while controlling for child age, sex, cognitive ability, and parental education, with preschool as random intercepts
Results showed an association of receptive vocabulary with NWR performance only. These findings suggest that NWR performance in preschool children may be relatively independent of individual differences in linguistic background and exposure, while being moderately associated with lexical development.

articles_hidden.title: A Comparative Study of Experiential and Distributional Representations for Concrete and Abstract Concepts
articles_hidden.authors: Laxmi R. Iyer; Martin Takac; Igor Farkas
articles_hidden.abstract:
We investigate the semantic distinction between concrete and abstract concepts by
examining the relative contribution of experiential (grounded) features and distributional
(language-based) features in modeling their representation via data driven analysis using
Spearman’s correlation between human similarity ratings, representational similarity
analysis between various feature spaces, multidimensional scaling, and category similarity.
Our results reveal a robust double dissociation between feature types and concept classes.
Grounded features better align with human judgements for concrete concepts than for
abstract concepts. Concrete concepts exhibit higher representational similarity across
different independently obtained grounded feature representations. In contrast, language
based features better align with human judgements for abstract concepts than for concrete
concepts. Abstract concepts exhibit higher representational similarity across different
independently obtained distributional feature representations. Multidimensional scaling
analyses further show that abstract concepts occupy a compressed and highly clustered
region in experiential space, with clustering driven more by degree of abstractness than
semantic similarity. Concrete concepts in contrast are highly correlated with sensorimotor
features in experiential space. Further, better category similarity for concrete concepts is
exhibited by experiential features rather than distributional features.

articles_hidden.title: Young Children’s Help-Seeking Expectations in Teacher-Child Interactions:  The Effects of Teachers’ Familiarity and Response Valence
articles_hidden.authors: Yilun Zhao; YUAN SHEN; Tianxin Song; Wenshuo Li; Ke Shen; anonymous; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective help-seeking is essential for young children’s adaptation in early childhood education settings, yet little is known about how they selectively seek help based on different social cues. This study examined how young children integrate teachers’ familiarity and response valence when predicting a protagonist’s help-seeking behavior. Across two studies, 90 Han Chinese children aged 4–6 years (45 boys) completed a third-party task simulating teacher-child interactions. In Study 1, familiarity was manipulated using photographs of each child’s real teachers, whereas Study 2 employed standardized cartoon figures and verbal cues to indicate familiarity. The results showed that children tended to expect that the protagonist would seek help from familiar teachers, especially those who responded positively. Meanwhile, they hesitated to expect that the protagonist would seek help from unfamiliar teachers, regardless of their response valence. This pattern indicates that familiarity consistently exerted a stronger influence than response valence, as children consistently prioritized familiarity when anticipating support. Together, these findings highlight how young children flexibly integrate multiple social cues when forming help-seeking expectations and offer practical implications for fostering secure, responsive teacher-child relationships in early education.

articles_hidden.title: Age-of-acquisition Effects across the Adult Lifespan: Evidence from Eye Movements in Compound Word Reading
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: The Age of Acquisition (AoA) effect is where words acquired during childhood are recognised more quickly than those acquired during adulthood. However, the influence of AoA on compound words and its stability across the adult lifespan remain under-investigated. We conducted two eye-tracking experiments to clarify how the AoA effect is moderated by ageing and spacing. Ninety British English adults participated across two eye-tracking experiments: 60 young adults (30 reading unspaced compounds in Experiment 1 and 30 reading spaced compounds in Experiment 2) and 30 older adults (who read both unspaced and spaced compounds across experiments). Using Bayesian linear mixed-effects models, we observed a robust AoA effect in both spaced and unspaced compound words in young adults. However, in older adults, we only observed an AoA effect in unspaced compound words. The AoA effect declined with increasing age, whereas the slope of AoA effect was shallower in spaced than unspaced compound words. These findings suggest that the functional influence of AoA is contingent upon orthographic structure and reading experience: while whole-word AoA influences processing across visual formats in younger readers, older readers shift away from whole-word lexical properties toward constituent-level strategies when orthographic structure is disrupted by spacing.
